sources.news_title: Four on death row for Richmond murders are among 548 spared by Gov. Newsom
sources.text:
Sign up for WhatMatters to receive the latest news and commentary on the most important issues in the Golden State.
By Jeanne Kuang and Nigel Duara
Gov. Gavin Newsom is commuting the death sentences of 548 people, including 10 who were convicted in Contra Costa County, clearing the state’s death row for the first time since the hangings were conducted in the late 19th century.
It is a monumental move in the history of capital punishment in America: The prisoners represent more than a quarter of the nation’s condemned inmates.
And it is a decision Newsom has spoken about in starkly personal terms. In 2019, shortly after taking office, he issued a moratorium on executions just three years after voters rejected a ballot measure to abolish the death penalty and instead approved one to speed them up. But at the time, the governor said he couldn’t be responsible for killing another person.
“After nearly 30 years in office I have come to understand the limits of what government can justly accomplish,” Newsom wrote in a letter addressed “to all Californians.” “I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values, undermines the foundations of our legal system, and diminishes each of us.”
Three of the 548 convicts who stand to receive a reprieve were convicted of committing murders in Richmond: Nathan Burris, who killed Deborah Ross and Ersie Everette at the Richmond-San Rafael Bridge toll plaza in 2009; Willie Darnell Johnson, who was convicted of murdering Willie Womble and attempting to kill Angela Womble during a 1986 home robbery; and Michael Nevail Pearson, who murdered coworkers Ruth Talley and Barbara Garcia after being fired from his Richmond Housing Authority job in 1995. The fourth involved John Sapp, a Concord man who was convicted of murdering Richmond resident Elizabeth Duarte on Mount Diablo.
Since 2024, death row has been a metaphorical place. The male prisoners were cleared out of their individual cells in San Quentin State Prison and distributed among other 24 facilities. Twenty female prisoners condemned to death were moved to general population at the Central California Women’s Facility that year.
Even before Newsom’s 2019 moratorium, it had been more than a decade since the state performed an execution. His successor, Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra, has committed to extending the moratorium when he takes office.
It is not unusual for governors or presidents to commute sentences on their way out of office. Then-President Joe Biden commuted the sentences of 37 of the 40 federal death row prisoners in 2024. But Newsom’s decision stands out as the largest act of mass clemency in U.S. history, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.
It comes as he decides whether to run for president after his term ends at the end of the year. Along with other signature Newsom moves like his early recognition of same-sex marriages as San Francisco mayor in 2004, it could boost his standing among Democrats as a bold actor pushing forward liberal causes, while inviting criticism from the center and right and from tougher-on-crime advocates.
Already, anti-death penalty groups have released an ad invoking Martin Luther King, Jr. that praises Newsom’s move as “rooted in justice, guided by conscience and made with courage.” Dan Newman, a Democratic strategist who works with those groups and also advises Newsom, said the governor made his decision without his political team and that Newsom did not know about the ad.
Dan Newman, a Democratic strategist who works with those groups and also advises Newsom, said the governor made his decision without his political team and that Newsom did not know about the ad.
Most of the decisions Newsom made Thursday will need court approval. For those convicted of multiple felonies — nearly 400 prisoners — four of seven judges on the California Supreme Court will have to sign off on the commutations.
Newsom said those with the commuted sentences will not be eligible for new Board of Parole Hearings commutation and resentencing regulations. That addresses some concerns prosecutors, victims’ groups and supporters of the death penalty had expressed as they anticipated Newsom’s decision: that those newly sentenced to life might get a chance later to be released.
“These offenders will die in prison but not by our hand,” Newsom wrote.
His anticipated decision garnered sharp condemnation in recent weeks from those groups, who argued it flew in the face of juries and judges that had upheld the death sentences, and voters who have upheld the practice.
“I don’t think he or any person should undo the sentence rendered by a jury and signed off by a judge because of his personal beliefs or feelings,” said Topo Padilla, president of Crime Victims United, last week.
Newsom said in his letter that the decision is among the most difficult of his career, “not because I doubt its necessity for our state but because I know its announcement may surface excruciating memories for victims’ families.” He said after meeting with them over the years, he considered commuting only some sentences but “that attempting to distinguish among crimes and offenders for clemency would inadvertently create two classes of murder victims — those whose perpetrators deserve the death penalty and then the rest.”
California has not executed a prisoner since Arnold Schwarzenegger was governor. Tookie Williams in 2005 and Clarence Ray Allen in 2006 were the last to die by execution at San Quentin State Prison.
Newsom inherited a very different prison system than Schwarzenegger’s marked by a rapidly decreasing incarcerated population. He moved to close five prisons so far, including a facility in Norco that was shut in October, and refashioned San Quentin as a hub for rehabilitation.
Advocate for victims pledges to challenge commutations
Anne Marie Schubert, chief executive of the Criminal Justice Legal Foundation and a former prosecutor, pledged that her group would challenge Newsom’s proposed commutations in the state Supreme Court. She said victims’ families were not notified of the proposed commutations.
“I find it atrocious and disrespectful and the most grotesque violation of victims’ rights I’ve ever seen,” Schubert said. “There’s 548 people on death row. That’s no less than 548 families that have been destroyed by what these people have done to their loved ones.”
Natasha Minsker, former director of the American Civil Liberties Union of California’s Center for Advocacy and Policy, said the death penalty is now a forgotten part of California politics. “I’m shocked, when I talk to legislators and tell them to oppose it, they say we don’t have the death penalty in California,” she said.
Mary McComb, the former state public defender, said from her first case defending a man with intellectual disabilities who was charged with a capital offense, she has found a moral reason to oppose the death penalty.
“One can always hope, but without the commutations, it’s not always guaranteed that governors would continue to have the courage to (maintain a moratorium),” McComb said.
Newsom’s commutations will affect prisoners convicted in some of the state’s most notorious killings, including Richard Allen Davis, whose slaying of 12-year-old Polly Klaas shook the Bay Area in the 1990s; Charles Ng, who was convicted of killing 11 people in the Sierra Nevada foothills in the 1980s; and Scott Peterson; whose murder of his pregnant wife Laci Peterson in Modesto drove tabloid headlines.
In an interview before the decision was made, Polly Klaas’ father Marc Klaas said the prospect of the commutations “upsets me terribly.” After years of appeals, Klaas said he had already given up the expectation that Davis would be executed one day, at the time of Newsom’s moratorium.
“But I was still secure in my mind that he and the rest of them would be on death row for the rest of their lives,” he said. “It’s so discouraging. It makes me feel terrible and it regurgitates all my personal feelings.”
Davis’ case is among those that Newsom is submitting to the Supreme Court for approval.
Polly’s sister feels differently. She said in a statement Thursday that she used to think Davis deserved execution but came to realize that his killing won’t help her recovery or public safety.
“The system tells survivors that execution matters to our healing. It doesn’t. It’s a distraction from what we actually need,” said Jess Nichol.

Richmondside Editor-in-Chief Kari Hulac contributed to this report.

In one of his last hurrahs before terming out as California’s governor, Gavin Newsom commuted the sentences of 568 incarcerated people on death row. They will now serve life in prison without the possibility of parole.
In a letter addressed to “all Californians” Thursday, Newsom said that, after his nearly 30 years in public office, he has “come to understand the limits of what government can justly accomplish.”
“I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values, undermines the foundations of our legal system, and diminishes each of us,” he wrote.
One of Newsom’s ongoing pushes while in office has been against the death penalty, and he formalized an existing moratorium on carrying out executions upon taking office in 2019.
A de facto moratorium was signed in 2006, when the last execution took place in California.
In his letter, Newsom acknowledged that his decision could stoke painful memories and spur strong reactions for victims’ families.
“I deeply respect the views of those who will strongly disagree with my decision, including some families of victims who have suffered the worst possible loss,” he wrote. “Today I am acting on my long and deeply held conviction that individually and collectively we are stronger as a society when we reject state-sanctioned killing.”
While this move prevents these currently incarcerated people from being put on death row again if a future governor ends the moratorium, it does not prevent future death row sentencing or resulting executions.
With Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra set to take office in January, the concern of this happening is low.
During his time as California attorney general, Becerra voiced support for the death penalty. But on the campaign trail, he confirmed that he would continue to support the moratorium that is in place.
This move from an exiting Newsom comes as a particularly horrifying aspect of the death penalty has reared its head.
Related | Republican suggests more ‘hurtful methods’ in Tennessee execution
In Tennessee, two execution attempts on Tony Carruthers and Christa Pike were botched just months apart from each other.
For Carruthers, who was convicted in connection with three murders in 1994, the execution was called off when medical staffers were reportedly unable to find a suitable vein to administer a lethal injection.
Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee issued a reprieve, ruling that Carruthers’ execution would be delayed for a year.
Human rights organizations have argued that Carruthers was wrongly convicted.
For Christa Pike, who was convicted of murder in 1995, her execution turned into what has been called “torture” as two separate doses of lethal injection failed.
“There hasn’t been a moment since that night when I haven’t been in pain,” Pike said in a statement obtained by The New York Times. “My body hurts. My arms hurt. My hands hurt. My throat hurts. I still struggle to speak.”
Following the incident with Pike, Gov. Lee paused all executions for the remainder of his term. Sen. Marsha Blackburn will be succeeding Lee come January, and the incoming governor has not only supported the death penalty, but supported expedited procedures and bringing back the electric chair.

Gavin Newsom Faces Backlash Over Decision to Commute All California Death Row Sentences — As Critics Question Timing Amid Presidential Rumors
Nov. 5 2026, Published 6:25 p.m. ET
California Governor Gavin Newsom has taken the unprecedented step of commuting every California death sentence to a sentence of life in prison without parole, RadarOnline.com can report.
The outgoing state leader's order affects all 548 prisoners on death row in the state in what will be one of the Democrat's final acts in office.
Gavin Newsom Ends Death Sentences in California
California has not put a prisoner to death since Jan. 17, 2006, when Clarence Ray Allen was executed via lethal injection.
However, Newsom, who many political pundits believe could be a frontrunner for president in 2028, explained in an open letter to his constituents, "I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California's values, undermines the foundations of our legal system, and diminishes each of us."
Newsom has long been a vocal opponent of capital punishment, which he believes is "morally objectionable." The 59-year-old slammed the death penalty as "unfair, unjust (and) wasteful" in an executive order signed in 2019, which imposed a moratorium on all executions, withdrew the state’s lethal injection protocol, and closed San Quentin’s execution chamber.
If his shocking declaration survives the inevitable legal and political challenges, it would empty the nation's largest death row and eliminate about a quarter of all death sentences nationwide.
However, there are already questions about whether or not he is actually allowed to reduce every prisoner's sentence under California law.
Many Legal Questions Must Still Be Answered
According to the state constitution, the governor can only grant clemency and commute sentences for inmates who have been convicted of one felony. The California Supreme Court's approval is required to grant clemency to anyone convicted of a felony more than once.
This means the court would have to approve 382 of the commutations announced Thursday, or roughly 70 percent, according to numbers provided by Newsom's office.
Newsom admitted the decision will be met with fierce opposition, acknowledging, "The people sentenced to death in California caused indescribable suffering to victims, their families, communities, and our state as a whole. The harm they inflicted persists across generations.
"Many Californians feel that those who commit brutal crimes deserve to die. But as Governor, I have concluded the state cannot morally kill them."
Death Penalty Opponents Cheer the Annoucement
Newsom went on to admit the decision was "the most difficult of my career, not because I doubt the necessity for our state but because I know its announcement may surface excruciating memories for victims' families."
The politician explained, "Today I am acting on my long and deeply held conviction that individually and collectively we are stronger as a society when we reject state-sanctioned killing."
As expected, his announcement was met with immediate mixed reactions.
"This is a day that will be remembered in California’s history and resonate globally for years to come," Amnesty International USA Executive Director Nadia Daar said in a statement. "The death penalty should be abolished, everywhere. Today marks a significant moment for human rights in California and across the country."
Victim Family Members Call Announcement 'Unbelievably Disappointing'
However, family members of murdered victims of death row inmates found the announcement unfathomable.
Marc Klaas, whose 12-year-old daughter Polly was killed in 1993 by Richard Allen Davis, called Newsom's decision a "knife in the back" to him and other victims’ families who found the capital punishment sentences well justified.
"It's unbelievably disappointing," Klaas told NBC News. "I was told that when this guy was sentenced to death, that this was a system we can trust. But here we are, 33 years later, and it's a system we can't trust."
Klass also noted the suspicious timing of Newsom's decree.
"We’re talking about serial killers, we're talking about spree killers, we're talking about cop killers, we're talking about child killers," he said. "Why, two days after the midterms, does Gavin Newsom feel the need to commute these sentences? Who benefits from this?"

sources.news_title: California Governor Gavin Newsom Commuting More Than 500 Inmates' Death Sentences To Life In Prison Without Parole
sources.text:
California Governor Gavin Newsom announced that he is commuting more than 500 death sentences to life without parole for inmates in the state. The governor made the announcement on Thursday, November 5, following the blue wave that dominated the midterm elections nationwide.
RELATED: Christa Pike’s Lawyers Reportedly Warned Court Of Rare Blood Cancer Diagnosis Prior To Execution Attempt (UPDATE)
California Governor Gavin Newsom Commutes 548 Death Sentences To Life
California Governor Gavin Newsom is commuting all death sentences in the state to life without parole. The governor made the announcement in a press release on Thursday, and he stated that the death sentences of 548 prisoners will be commuted. The Democratic governor cited the “imperfect legal system” in his announcement.
“To All Californians,” reads the release. “I have decided to exercise my constitutional clemency authority to commute all California death sentences to life without the possibility of parole. After nearly 30 years in public office, I have come to understand the limits of what government can justly accomplish. I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values, undermines the foundations of our legal system, and diminishes each of us. I know we cannot execute people in our imperfect legal system and remain true to our core values, first among them justice and human decency. My decision today comes after nearly three decades of openly opposing state-sanctioned executions as an elected official. Soon after taking office as Governor of California, on March 13, 2019, I instituted a moratorium on executions. I could not remain true to my values and oversee the killing of people with death warrants in California. My action formalized the de facto moratorium on executions in place since 2006, the last year California executed anyone. While the moratorium has prevented any further executions, it left all death sentences in place. The 548 people now under sentence of death in California make up the largest death row in the Western Hemisphere.”
Stay Connected
Subscribe to updates from The Shade Room
Governor Newsom added that the decision was “among the most difficult” of his career, citing victims’ families. However, he also said that the state can not “morally kill them.”
“I deeply respect the views of those who will strongly disagree with my decision, including some families of victims who have suffered the worst possible loss,” he continued. “I hold this painful truth along with the belief that this is a righteous action. Today I am acting on my long and deeply held conviction that individually and collectively we are stronger as a society when we reject state-sanctioned killing… The harm they inflicted persists across generations. Many Californians feel that those who commit brutal crimes deserve to die. But as Governor, I have concluded the state cannot morally kill them.”
Newsom will grant clemency to 529 men and 19 women.
ACLU Responds With Statement
The Executive Director of the ACLU, Anthony Romero, celebrated the decision while citing “racism” and “inhumane punishment,” according to ABC7 Eyewitness News.
“These commutations reflect what justice demands,” said Romero. “An end to a racist, error-prone, and inhumane punishment that has burdened California for far too long.”
Black people are up to eight times more likely to receive a death sentence compared to non-Black defendants, according to the ACLU. In addition, Hispanic people are at least six times more likely to receive a death sentence.
Tennessee Botches Execution Of Death Row Inmate Christa Pike
The announcement comes mere weeks after Tennessee state Pike botched the execution of death row inmate Christa Pike. The Shade Room reported that Pike was given two injections of the lethal drug pentobarbital on Wednesday, September 30. The failed execution took place at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution. The drug is supposed to be fatal within 15 minutes to 30 minutes, but the 50-year-old survived both injections and was rushed to the emergency room.
Pike was reportedly diagnosed with the vein condition thrombocytosis, which her lawyers argued would make locating a vein difficult. She said at the time of the failed execution, “My arm feels like it’s about to burst open, per NBC News. The prison staff reportedly used at least 10 needles on Pike.
“Tonight the State of Tennessee once again failed to carry out a lawful execution,” reads a statement from attorneys Randy Spivey and Kelly Gleason. “We take no pleasure in being right, but the concerns raised by Ms. Pike proved to be true: difficult vein access, blown veins, degraded pentobarbital, no emergency medical care available when things inevitably go wrong, all under a protocol that remains veiled in secrecy.”
Pike spent a week unconscious and on a ventilator, and she later made a statement about the botched procedure.
“There hasn’t been a moment since that night when I haven’t been in pain,” she wrote, per WKRN. “My body hurts. My arms hurt. My hands hurt. My throat hurts. I still struggle to speak. And the pain isn’t just physical. There is pain in my mind and in my soul. I had not contemplated life beyond that night, and I’m deeply hurt by the incompetence that has put so many people in this terrible position.”
The state of Tennessee canceled the remaining executions for the year following the failed attempt. The state also failed to execute inmate Tony Carruthers earlier in 2026. The staff reportedly couldn’t locate a vein for the IV, according to WSFB. Dr. Mark Fowler oversaw both failed executions.

As one of his final acts in office, California Gov. Gavin Newsom has commuted the sentences of all 548 people sentenced to death in California to life without the possibility of parole—a quarter of the death row prisoners in the United States—he announced in a November 5 letter.
California has not executed anyone since 2006, when Republican Arnold Schwarzenegger was governor. Amid legal challenges to lethal injection protocols, executions were de facto paused for years. And shortly after Newsom took office in 2019, he instituted a formal moratorium on executions. Now, Newsom plans to empty what is still the largest death row in the Western Hemisphere.
“After nearly 30 years in public office, I have come to understand the limits of what government can justly accomplish,” Newsom, who is considered a likely 2028 presidential candidate, wrote Thursday. “I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values, undermines the foundations of our legal system, and diminishes each of us.”
The decision does not permanently repeal the death penalty—California is still one of 27 states that retain capital punishment, though Newsom’s newly elected successor Xavier Becerra has committed to extending the execution moratorium once he is in office. Newsom’s commutations must be individually approved by California’s courts.
The United States has executed 33 people in 2026 so far. It’s one of a few dozen nations that have the death penalty on the books—most of which, like California, do not actually carry out executions. According to Amnesty International, only 17 countries, including the US, executed anyone in 2025. Executions, even in the US, are increasingly unpopular—and, according to the Death Penalty Information Center, executing a person is consistently more expensive than other punishments.
Nonetheless, the current White House has encouraged an expansion of capital punishment in America, bringing back federal firing squads earlier this year and floating the idea of livestreaming an execution.
But the overwhelming majority of death row prisoners are held at the state level, like California’s, where governors hold the power of clemency. As Newsom wrote Tuesday: “I know we cannot execute people in our imperfect legal system and remain true to our core values, first among them justice and human decency.”

SACRAMENTO, Calif. (VVNG.com) — Gov. Gavin Newsom announced Thursday, November 5, 2026, that he has decided to commute all California death sentences to life in prison without the possibility of parole, drawing criticism from the San Bernardino County District Attorney’s Office.
In an open letter addressed to Californians, Newsom said the decision involves 548 people currently under sentence of death. He said he would issue the same commutation to every condemned person.
Locally, a review of the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation’s condemned inmate list, updated November 3, identified 39 people whose trial county is listed as San Bernardino. The designation identifies where their cases were tried, rather than their hometown or current prison location.
“I have decided to exercise my constitutional clemency authority to commute all California death sentences to life without the possibility of parole,” Newsom wrote.
The governor acknowledged that the process requires California Supreme Court review for people twice convicted of a felony. His letter does not state that all individual commutations have been completed.
In a written statement responding to the announcement, the San Bernardino County District Attorney’s Office called it “the wrong decision” and accused Newsom of prioritizing political ambitions over victims and their families.
“His commutations are solely based upon power and political aspirations,” the statement said.
The office specifically cited Josh Ryen and Mary Ann Hughes, whose families were affected by the killings for which Kevin Cooper was convicted. The statement said Newsom had not called either of them to seek their views on a potential commutation for Cooper.
The statement described Josh as a surviving victim who was left for dead and identified Hughes as the mother of Chris Hughes, who was killed.
The District Attorney’s Office also alleged that Newsom had failed to honor crime victims’ constitutional rights, including notification rights. The statement said the office was unaware of victims’ family members receiving notice of the commutations from the governor.
Those assertions were part of the office’s criticism; the materials provided for this article do not independently establish whether required notifications were issued.
The office further argued that blanket commutations disregard California voters’ support for retaining the death penalty and the decisions of jurors who imposed death sentences.
“These death sentences that the Governor is attempting to commute were all imposed by twelve members of the community,” the statement said.
Newsom addressed opposition from victims’ families in his letter, acknowledging that the announcement could revive painful memories and that some families would strongly disagree with his decision.
He said he had consulted crime victims and survivors, public safety experts, religious and civil rights leaders, prison wardens, and jurors who served in capital cases. Those people held differing views, he wrote.
Newsom framed his decision around his longstanding opposition to executions, concerns about wrongful convictions and his belief that California’s death penalty system cannot be administered fairly.
“By every measure, California’s system for administering the death penalty is a failure,” he wrote.
The announcement follows the execution moratorium Newsom instituted on March 13, 2019. According to the letter, that action prevented executions but left death sentences in place.
California’s last execution occurred on January 17, 2006, when Clarence Ray Allen was executed at San Quentin State Prison. Allen had been sentenced to death for masterminding a 1980 triple murder at a Fresno market and conspiring to murder witnesses who previously testified against him, according to state officials. www.cdcr.ca.gov
Newsom emphasized that the proposed commutations would not repeal California’s death penalty. His letter states that the action is limited to existing death sentences, while prosecutors, juries and courts retain their roles in seeking, imposing and upholding death sentences in individual cases.
The power to repeal the death penalty rests with the Legislature and voters, he wrote.
Newsom said he considered distinguishing among crimes and offenders when deciding who should receive clemency, but ultimately chose to apply the same punishment to everyone currently sentenced to death.
“These offenders will die in prison but not by our hand,” Newsom wrote.
The governor described the decision as among the most difficult of his career and acknowledged that it would anger and hurt some Californians.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom plans to commute the death sentences of all 548 inmates on death row in the state to life imprisonment without the possibility of parole.
The move is the largest clemency action in state history.
“After nearly 30 years in public office, I have come to understand the limits of what government can justly accomplish,” Newsom said.
“I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values, undermines the foundations of our legal system, and diminishes each of us. I know we cannot execute people in our imperfect legal system and remain true to our core values, first among them justice and human decency.”
Newsom declared a moratorium on executions in March 2019, soon after becoming governor. The last execution in the state took place in 2006 when Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger, a Republican, was in office.
The death penalty remains on the books in the Golden State, and a future governor could lift the moratorium, which would affect future death penalty cases. In 2016, state voters defeated a referendum to abolish capital punishment, while at the same time approving a measure that sought to speed up the death penalty appeals process.
Newsom’s announcement came after Tennessee’s failed attempt to execute convicted murderer Christa Pike on Sept. 30 raised questions about capital punishment and how it is carried out. Pike was hospitalized and returned to prison on Oct. 10.
The death penalty has also been in the spotlight after Secretary of War Pete Hegseth said the planned firing squad execution of mass murderer Nidal Hasan would be livestreamed.
President Donald Trump later said on social media that the execution would not be livestreamed. The president said streaming the event would show the world how the United States deals with terrorists, but “many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device.”
Hasan was convicted by a military court-martial of killing 13 people and wounding more than 30 at the Fort Hood military base in Texas in November 2009. Although he was not charged with terrorism, he told a military sanity board that shooting soldiers was a way in which he participated in jihad, or armed struggle in the name of Islam. It was the largest mass murder ever to occur at a U.S. military installation. The execution is scheduled for Dec. 3.

California Governor Gavin Newsom moves to change 548 death sentences to life without parole
California Governor Gavin Newsom has moved to change 548 death sentences to life in prison without the possibility of parole.
California Governor Gavin Newsom said Thursday that he’ll change more than 500 death sentences in the state to life in prison without the possibility of parole, though the state Supreme Court will have the final say in hundreds of those cases.
“I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values, undermines the foundations of our legal system, and diminishes each of us,” Newsom said in a public letter.
Newsom’s decision comes as he prepares to leave office after eight years and considers a run for president. The Democrat, who’s long been opposed to the death penalty, placed a moratorium on executions in California in 2019.
His latest move came after he realized “the limits of what government can justly accomplish,” he said.
Newsom moved to grant clemency to 548 people currently sentenced to death in California, of whom 529 are men and 19 are women, according to numbers provided by his office.
The state constitution requires the California Supreme Court’s approval to grant clemency to anyone convicted of a felony more than once, which means the court would have to approve 382 of those commutations, or roughly 70%, according to Newsom's office.

California voters upheld the death penalty
Americans have long been divided over the death penalty. Nearly half of U.S. states have banned capital punishment outright, but executions are still carried out routinely around the country. On Thursday alone, Florida, Alabama and Indiana had scheduled lethal injections.
Californians voted via ballot measures to uphold the death penalty in 2012 and 2016. No one has been executed in the state since 2006 and California has the largest death row in the Western Hemisphere.
Among the most notorious convicted killers on California’s death row are Richard Allen Davis, who kidnapped and murdered 12-year-old Polly Klaas in 1993, and Randy Kraft, the so-called “Scorecard Killer” who kept a list of his 16 victims in the 1970s and ’80s. Other prominent killers, including Scott Peterson and the Manson family members, received death sentences that were later commuted to life in prison.
Jess Nichol, Klaas' sister, said she previously believed Davis deserved the death penalty, but her views evolved.
“The system tells survivors that execution matters to our healing," Nichol said in a statement. "It doesn’t. It’s a distraction from what we actually need.”
Newsom said the decision was among the most difficult choices of his career because it will surface painful memories for crime victims’ families.
“As Governor, I alone bear responsibility for this decision and its impact, just as I alone would bear responsibility for each execution,” Newsom wrote.
Victims' groups and prosecutors decry the decision
Patricia Wenskunas, founder of the California advocacy nonprofit Crime Survivors, which opposed the abolition of the death penalty, criticized Newsom's decision.
“My heart hurts for every one of the victims and every one of their family members,” she said, calling the decision “offensive” and “outrageous.”
The California District Attorneys Association didn’t immediately comment on the announcement. But last month the group sent a letter to Newsom expressing “grave concerns” about him considering the move and warning that such a sweeping action would inflict additional anguish on victims’ families.
“To simply erase all those judgments with the stroke of a pen, without considering the facts of each case or the families affected, would be a profound disservice to the administration of justice,” association President Jeannine M. Pacioni said.
San Luis Obispo County District Attorney Dan Dow called the move a “sickening abuse of power.”
Dow referenced Rachel Newhouse and Aundria Crawford, two women who were kidnapped, raped and murdered by Rex Allan Krebs in 1999, and Kesha Gurke, a 19-month-old girl tortured and murdered by Michael Whisenhunt in 1995.
“San Luis Obispo County juries sentenced both men to death. A unanimous California Supreme Court affirmed both judgments. Their families have waited decades for the State of California to keep its word. Today, the Governor broke it,” Dow said.
Orange County District Attorney Todd Spitzer also condemned the decision, calling it “mercy for the wolves and while inflicting the ultimate act of cruelty on the sheep.”
The ACLU applauds the move
The American Civil Liberties Union, which has said the implementation of the death penalty reflects racial bias, applauded the announcement.
“These commutations reflect what justice demands: an end to a racist, error-prone, and inhumane punishment that has burdened California for far too long,” Executive Director Anthony Romero said in a statement.
The ACLU is involved in an ongoing legal challenge to California’s death penalty statute, alleging it is racially discriminatory and unconstitutional.
Newsom has said in the past that it is wrong for the government to kill its citizens and that capital punishment in practice has discriminated against mentally ill people and people of color.
Other governors have granted broad clemency to all death row prisoners in their states, including Gov. Kate Brown in Oregon in 2022 and Gov. Jared Polis in Colorado in 2020.
In 2024, President Joe Biden also granted clemency to 37 out of 40 federal prisoners sentenced to death.
Xavier Becerra, a Democrat who will take over from Newsom in January, has said he will extend the state’s moratorium on the death penalty.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom’s grant of clemency to the 548 people under a death sentence in his state is a singular event in the history of America’s death penalty. No other governor ever has come close to sparing that many lives.
Compare Newsom’s move to other governors who, in the last two decades, have cleared out their state’s death rows. In 2003, Illinois Gov. George Ryan commuted 167 death sentences and granted four pardons. Four years later, Jon Corzine commuted the sentences of the eight people on New Jersey’s death row. In 2011, another Illinois governor, Pat Quinn, commuted 15 death sentences, and in 2022, Oregon Gov. Kate Brown commuted 17. The magnitude of Newsom’s action today overshadows them all.
But it’s where death penalty sentences are headed. And as I have explained elsewhere, “Since 1977, governors in 24 states have granted capital clemency 327 times. Indeed, in only ten of the states that still retain the death penalty have governors not granted clemency during this timeframe. Three of them (California, Oregon and Pennsylvania) currently have a moratorium on executions, and another four of them have some of the smallest death rows in the country (Utah, South Dakota, Nebraska and Kansas).”
Newsom’s clemency reduced the total number of people on death rows across the country by more than a quarter. It comes in the wake of Christa Pike’s failed execution and at a time when capital punishment is very much on the minds of many Americans.
Newsom’s reasons for granting universal clemency are compelling. He has described the state’s death penalty system as “unfair, unjust, wasteful, protracted.” As he explained, “Death sentences are unevenly and unfairly applied to people of color, people with mental disabilities, and people who cannot afford costly legal representation.” And the governor noted that “innocent people have been sentenced to death in California.”
Those reasons echo concerns expressed by the other governors who have granted mass clemencies to people under death sentences. For example, as Oregon’s Brown explained when she exercised that power, the death penalty is “an irreversible punishment that does not allow for correction; is wasteful of taxpayer dollars; does not make communities safer; and cannot be and never has been administered fairly and equitably.”
Illinois’ Quinn commuted all existing death sentences the same day he signed a bill abolishing capital punishment in his state. He said: “Since our experience has shown that there is no way to design a perfect death penalty system, free from the numerous flaws that can lead to wrongful convictions or discriminatory treatment, I have concluded that the proper course of action is to abolish it. With our broken system, we cannot ensure that justice is achieved in every case.”
But unlike Brown’s and Quinn’s efforts, more work is needed to complete what Newsom started. Under a California law governing clemency, the California Supreme Court has to approve the commutations of any of the 548 people with multiple felony convictions. This provision was added to the state constitution in 1879, as an alternative to a proposal to forbid the governor from using their clemency power in cases where an offender had committed more than one felony. But it was clear at the time it was adopted that it did not empower “the justices of the court to supplement or supplant the Governor’s executive clemency authority.”
In 2018, the California Supreme Court explained that the idea was that “the court could serve as a check on the Governor within the confines of its traditional judicial role, determining whether there exists a legitimate basis on which the Governor could choose to grant clemency to the applicant.” As the court put it, “Article V, Section 8 of the California Constitution does not require the justices of this court to determine whether, in the view of each justice, an applicant deserves clemency, whether based on claimed innocence of the crime, rehabilitation, mercy, or other grounds.”
The court’s role is exceedingly limited. The justices ask only whether the governor’s actions are an “abuse” of his broad constitutional authority, such as corruption or conflict of interest. The court’s narrow role is consistent with its long-standing view that the governor’s clemency power is “virtually unlimited.”
And as an amicus brief filed by California’s death penalty defense agencies observes that “commuting some, but less than all, death sentences would not remedy the injustices the Governor wishes to address; it would make them worse.” The brief argues that since Newsom has made clear that in view of the systemic problems that have long plagued California’s death penalty system, “universal clemency based on systemic factors is more appropriate than grants of clemency based on individual circumstances … the clemency grants he has asked this Court to recommend would buttress those he has already unilaterally issued, to complete his goal.”
In addition, the state Supreme Court has regularly approved gubernatorial clemency decisions. In the past few months, it has given the green light to commutations of sentences of life without parole so that they “can be eligible for a parole suitability hearing.”
Now, the California Supreme Court has a chance to complete Newsom’s use of the clemency power to spare lives. It should do so expeditiously. When the court approves it, Gov. Newsom will move California, and the United States, one step closer to ridding itself of capital punishment.

sources.text:
California Gov. Gavin Newsom announced Thursday that he would commute all death sentences in the state to life imprisonment, a sweeping move affecting more than 500 death row inmates.
Newsom, who is widely expected to make a run for the White House in 2028, said capital punishment was "incompatible" with the values of the most populous state in the U.S.
"Today I am acting on my long and deeply held conviction that individually and collectively we are stronger as a society when we reject state-sanctioned killing," he wrote in a letter addressed "to all Californians."
With 548 people awaiting execution in California, the state has one of the largest death row populations in the world.
However, it has not carried out a death sentence for two decades, even as courts continue to impose the penalty on those convicted of murder and other serious crimes.
"Many Californians feel that those who commit brutal crimes deserve to die. But as governor, I have concluded the state cannot morally kill them," he said, calling the decision "among the most difficult of my career."
"I do, however, pray that this action will finally separate the memories of the victims of these crimes from the fate of those who harmed them. We can now let these offenders die in obscurity while we forever remember and honor their victims."
The announcement comes with a renewed spotlight on the death penalty in the U.S., one of the few wealthy countries to retain the punishment.
In September, the state of Tennessee failed twice to kill convicted murderer Christa Pike with a lethal injection before rushing her to hospital in a drama that made headlines around the world.
Last month, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced that the firing squad execution of a man who went on a shooting rampage at an army base would be livestreamed.
Days later and after an outcry from both sides of the political aisle, as well as from the Catholic Church and the United Nations, President Donald Trump cancelled the plan, saying Nidal Hasan would still die, but that the sentence would not be broadcast.
In a lengthy letter on Thursday, Newsom appeared to be walking the public through his thought process and the discussions he said he has had on the issue.
He said the decision to issue a blanket commutation for all death row inmates came down to not differentiating among those affected by heinous acts.
"I have concluded that attempting to distinguish among crimes and offenders for clemency would inadvertently create two classes of murder victims – those whose perpetrators deserve the death penalty and then the rest.
"I will therefore issue the same commutation to every condemned person - life without the possibility of parole, the most severe punishment I can lawfully impose and the state of California can ethically enforce. These offenders will die in prison but not by our hand."

“Many Californians feel that those who commit brutal crimes deserve to die,” Newsom said in his letter. “But as Governor, I have concluded the state cannot morally kill them.”
He called the state’s death penalty system “a failure” that “has not been and cannot be fairly applied and has resulted in the conviction of innocent people”.
“I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values, undermines the foundation of our legal system, and diminishes each of us,” the Governor said.
The state does not allow a Governor to unilaterally commute the sentence of those with numerous felony convictions outside their capital murder cases, which account for about 70% of the state’s death row prisoners.
In those cases, the state Supreme Court will need to review Newsom’s clemency grants. At least four of the court’s seven justices must sign off on the commutation for it to take effect.
Newsom wrote that he is “confident” the mass commutation is consistent with California law, but acknowledged this act of clemency requires the court to “participate in a weighty decision they did not choose to take up and with which they may personally disagree”.
California has not carried out an execution since 2006.
Newsom’s decision drew strong reactions from the families of murder victims. Some of them have openly supported commutations, while others have viscerally opposed the possibility.
Before the announcement, some district attorneys and victim advocates urged the Governor to leave death row alone – and hinted at legal challenges if he issued a mass commutation.
The move could have political repercussions, too, as critics come after Newsom and other Democrats for their criminal justice policies. But commuting the sentences could also win him credit with those weary of the justice system and reform advocates who have long been concerned about wrongful convictions and documented racial disparities in death sentences.
Newsom acknowledged that tension in his letter, writing that he understands his move will “anger and hurt some Californians”. He described seeking counsel from crime victims, public safety experts and religious and civil rights leaders.
“I deeply respect the views of those who will strongly disagree with my decision, including some families of victims who have suffered the worst possible loss,” Newsom wrote. “I hold this painful truth along with the belief that this is a righteous action.”
Governors in other states, including Oregon and Illinois, have commuted their own death rows, but none were nearly as large as California’s.
Shortly before leaving office, President Joe Biden commuted the sentences of 37 of the 40 people on federal death row, a move that has drawn sharp criticism from President Donald Trump and his allies.
While the death penalty used to be widely popular nationwide, support for it has dropped significantly. Still, despite a decline in executions nationwide, the pace of state-sanctioned killings has accelerated recently in some Republican-led states as the Trump administration has pushed for more capital punishment.
The district and 23 states have abolished the death penalty, according to the Death Penalty Information Centre, but it remains on the books in 27 states and the federal system.
Five of those states currently have moratoriums blocking executions – including Tennessee, where Governor Bill Lee paused them this autumn after prison officials botched the lethal injection of convicted killer Christa Pike. Her unprecedented survival of two doses of pentobarbital is the subject of ongoing litigation and an independent investigation.
In four death penalty states currently led by Republicans, Democrats will take over next year, potentially setting the stage for additional executive moves curtailing capital punishment.
Throughout his political career, Newsom has been clear on his strong opposition to the death penalty. He imposed a moratorium on executions in March 2019 and closed the state’s death chamber at San Quentin State Prison, moving those on death row into the general prison population.
“My ultimate goal is to end the death penalty in California,” Newsom said at the time.
His mass commutation effectively does just that, for now, though the death penalty remains legal and prosecutors in some counties are still pursuing capital cases.
In a letter to Newsom ahead of his decision, Dan Dow, district attorney of San Luis Obispo County, wrote that a universal act of clemency would rob victims’ families of the individual consideration their cases warranted.
Dow has also repeatedly emphasised his belief that any act of clemency – including this mass commutation – should explicitly acknowledge the names of the people killed by those on California’s death row.
In a statement on Thursday (local time), Dow lambasted Newsom for not naming any capital murder victims, including the three from his county.
“Governor Newsom just told the families of Rachel Newhouse, Aundria Crawford, Kesha Gurke and every other innocent victim of California’s 548 condemned killers that the killers’ lives matter more,” Dow said. “Juries chose justice case by case, voters chose it five times, and one outgoing governor is trying to erase it all with a pen. This is a sickening abuse of power.”
Before Thursday’s announcement, the Governor had been openly wrestling with the idea and said on his podcast last month that he had lots of “people in my ear” saying not to do it.
But he told guest Bryan Stevenson, a prominent lawyer and death penalty opponent, that he was thinking hard about the issue.
“I have to prepare for my own conscience, my rocking chair test,” Newsom told Stevenson. “Do I commute the largest death row in the Western Hemisphere?”
“I think you do,” Stevenson answered, “and I think it becomes a really pivotal moment in this country.”

California death row sentences to be commuted to life without parole, Newsom says
Gov. Gavin Newsom says he will commute every current death sentence in California to life in prison without the possibility of parole.
Newsom announced the decision Thursday in an open letter, saying he will use his constitutional clemency authority to commute the sentences of 548 people currently facing the death penalty.
"I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California's values, undermines the foundations of our legal system, and diminishes each of us," Newsom wrote.
The move does not repeal California's death penalty or prevent prosecutors from seeking it in future cases. Newsom said those decisions will remain with prosecutors, juries and courts.
"Many Californians feel that those who commit brutal crimes deserve to die. But as Governor, I have concluded the state cannot morally kill them," Newsom wrote.
California voters, however, have repeatedly chosen to keep the death penalty.
Voters rejected Proposition 34, which would have abolished capital punishment, in 2012. Four years later, they again rejected repeal with Proposition 62 while narrowly approving Proposition 66, which sought to speed up death penalty cases.
Newsom imposed a moratorium on executions shortly after taking office in 2019. California last carried out an execution in 2006.
The decision drew sharply different reactions from California criminal justice officials.
Los Angeles County Public Defender Ricardo García praised the move, saying his office had called for universal clemency because of what he described as deep inequities in the death penalty system.
"Clemency is not leniency," García said in a statement. "This decision moves California closer to a justice system that values human dignity."
Orange County District Attorney Todd Spitzer strongly criticized the commutations, saying they override verdicts reached by juries and undermine the wishes of crime victims' families.
"The pursuit of justice does not bend to political whims, and I am heartbroken for the hundreds of families who must now grapple with the devastation of knowing that the monsters who harmed their loved ones are one step closer to being back out on our streets," Spitzer stated.
Spitzer said his office will continue seeking the death penalty in cases where prosecutors believe it is warranted.
Under the commutations announced Thursday, every current death sentence would instead become life without parole, which Newsom called the most severe punishment he can impose through clemency.
Some cases will require review by the California Supreme Court because the state constitution requires court approval before a governor can grant clemency to someone convicted of more than one felony.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom said Thursday that he’ll change more than 500 death sentences in the state to life in prison without the possibility of parole, though the state Supreme Court will have the final say in hundreds of those cases.
“I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values, undermines the foundations of our legal system, and diminishes each of us,” Newsom said in a public letter.
Newsom’s decision comes as he prepares to leave office after eight years and considers a run for president. The Democrat, who’s long been opposed to the death penalty, placed a moratorium on executions in California in 2019.
Related video above: Newsom says he will commute all death sentences in California to life without possibility of parole
His latest move came after he realized “the limits of what government can justly accomplish,” he said.
Newsom moved to grant clemency to 548 people currently sentenced to death in California, of whom 529 are men and 19 are women, according to numbers provided by his office.
The state constitution requires the California Supreme Court’s approval to grant clemency to anyone convicted of a felony more than once, which means the court would have to approve 382 of those commutations, or roughly 70%, according to Newsom's office.
According to the Death Penalty Information Center, Newsom’s action represents the largest mass clemency in American history. If they are all approved, it would reduce the U.S. death row population by nearly 30%, the center said.
California voters upheld the death penalty
Americans have long been divided over the death penalty. Nearly half of U.S. states have banned capital punishment outright, but executions are still carried out routinely around the country. On Thursday alone, Florida, Alabama and Indiana carried out lethal injections.
Californians voted to uphold the death penalty in 2012 and 2016 ballot measures. No one has been executed in the state since 2006 and California has the largest death row in the Western Hemisphere.
Among the most notorious convicted killers on California’s death row are Richard Allen Davis, who kidnapped and murdered 12-year-old Polly Klaas in 1993, and Randy Kraft, the so-called “Scorecard Killer” who kept a list of his 16 victims in the 1970s and ’80s. Other prominent killers, including Scott Peterson and the Manson family members, received death sentences that were later commuted to life in prison.
Jess Nichol, Klaas' sister, said she previously believed Davis deserved the death penalty, but her views evolved.
“The system tells survivors that execution matters to our healing,” Nichol said in a statement. “It doesn’t. It’s a distraction from what we actually need.”
Newsom said the decision was among the most difficult choices of his career because it will surface painful memories for crime victims’ families.
“As Governor, I alone bear responsibility for this decision and its impact, just as I alone would bear responsibility for each execution,” Newsom wrote.
The American Civil Liberties Union, which has said the implementation of the death penalty reflects racial bias, applauded the announcement.
“These commutations reflect what justice demands: an end to a racist, error-prone, and inhumane punishment that has burdened California for far too long,” Executive Director Anthony Romero said in a statement.
The ACLU is involved in an ongoing legal challenge to California’s death penalty statute, alleging it is racially discriminatory and unconstitutional.
Victims' groups and prosecutors decry the decision
Patricia Wenskunas, founder of the California advocacy nonprofit Crime Survivors, which opposed the abolition of the death penalty, criticized Newsom's decision.
“My heart hurts for every one of the victims and every one of their family members,” she said, calling the decision “offensive” and “outrageous.”
Steve Herr, whose son Sam Herr was murdered along with his friend Julie Kibuishi by Daniel Wozniak in 2010, said he was “absolutely disgusted” by the governor's decision. He said the death of his son's killer would have meant closure.
“When somebody commits such a heinous crime, they do not deserve to live,” Herr said. “To hear what Newsom just did … he’s just an outright coward.”
The California District Attorneys Association condemned the decision. Last month, the group sent a letter to Newsom expressing “grave concerns” about him considering the move and warning that such a sweeping action would inflict additional pain on victims’ relatives.
“With the stroke of a pen, Governor Newsom has disregarded the decisions of hundreds of jurors and judges, and the anguish of families who lost loved ones to the worst crimes imaginable,” CDAA President Jeannine M. Pacioni said in a statement. “The victims were never given a commutation. Their families were never given a choice. They deserve far better than this.”
San Luis Obispo County District Attorney Dan Dow called the move a “sickening abuse of power.”
Dow referenced Rachel Newhouse and Aundria Crawford, two women who were kidnapped, raped and murdered by Rex Allan Krebs in 1999, and Kesha Gurke, a 19-month-old girl tortured and murdered by Michael Whisenhunt in 1995.
“San Luis Obispo County juries sentenced both men to death. A unanimous California Supreme Court affirmed both judgments. Their families have waited decades for the State of California to keep its word. Today, the Governor broke it,” Dow said.
Orange County District Attorney Todd Spitzer also condemned the decision, calling it “mercy for the wolves and while inflicting the ultimate act of cruelty on the sheep.”
Other governors have taken similar actions
Newsom has said in the past that it is wrong for the government to kill its citizens and that capital punishment in practice has discriminated against mentally ill people and people of color.
Other governors have granted broad clemency to all death row prisoners in their states, including Gov. Kate Brown in Oregon in 2022 and Gov. Jared Polis in Colorado in 2020. Both are Democrats. In 1986, then-New Mexico Gov. Toney Anaya, a Democrat, commuted the death sentences of all five inmates then on death row.
In 2024, President Joe Biden also granted clemency to 37 out of 40 federal prisoners sentenced to death.
Xavier Becerra, a Democrat who will take over from Newsom in January, has said he will extend the state’s moratorium on the death penalty.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom announced Thursday he is commuting every death sentence in his state to a sentence of life in prison without parole – nearly eight years after declaring a moratorium on executions.
“My decision today comes after nearly three decades of openly opposing state-sanctioned executions as an elected official,” Newsom, who is mulling a 2028 White House bid, wrote in an open letter to California residents shared by his office.
The move will impact the lives of 548 people in the state, which has the largest number of people under a death sentence in the United States, according to the Death Penalty Information Center, a nonprofit that tracks capital punishment. The state’s last execution took place about 20 years ago.
Newsom’s announcement comes as the death penalty faces renewed scrutiny following Tennessee’s failed execution of Christa Pike in late September.
In the weeks since Pike survived two doses of pentobarbital, Tennessee paused the state’s remaining executions but requests to stop executions elsewhere have been denied in courts. Three lethal injections were scheduled on Thursday, with Florida and Alabama planning to execute two men hours after an execution in Indiana.
Taking hundreds of people off death row won’t be automatic. There are 382 cases the California Supreme Court will need to review and approve the commutation, according to the governor’s office. Those cases involve prisoners with more than one felony conviction.
California’s death row prisoners include serial killers Randy Kraft, also known as the “Southern California Strangler”; Charles Ng, who was convicted of killing 11 people in California in the 1980s; and Richard Allen Davis, who kidnapped and killed 12-year-old Polly Klaas in 1993.
‘A historic step’
The American Civil Liberties Union in a statement Thursday praised Newsom’s decision, saying it marks “a historic step towards ending the death penalty in California and across the country.”
“These commutations reflect what justice demands: an end to a racist, error-prone, and inhumane punishment that has burdened California for far too long,” said Anthony D. Romero, ACLU executive director. “By taking this step, Gov. Newsom has affirmed that the death penalty has no place in California and he showed real courage by confronting racialized injustice head-on.”
Other groups, including the Criminal Justice Legal Foundation, Crime Survivors and the California District Attorneys Association opposed the move, saying it would harm victims’ families and undermine the will of California and the court system.
“Our hearts break for every family feeling revictimized by this decision. You deserve to be heard, respected, and your loved ones will always be remembered,” Crime Survivors said in a statement.
Meanwhile, some victims’ families on Thursday expressed support for Newsom’s decision.
“I used to think the man who killed my sister deserved execution,” Jess Nichol, sister of Polly Klaas, who was killed in 1993, said in a statement. “But over time I’ve realized that whether he’s executed has absolutely nothing to do with my recovery or with real public safety.”
California has executed 13 people since 1976, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.
Only five people received death sentences in 2025, down from 42 in 1999. As of April of this year, 68% of people under a death sentence in California were defendants of color, according to the center.
Death penalty remains a divisive issue
Newsom’s announcement prompted a range of reactions from California prosecutors.
Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan J. Hochman said that while commuting death sentences is within Newsom’s power, completely eliminating the death penalty is still in the voters’ hands.
“Californians have been asked on two separate ballot initiatives to abolish the death penalty and both times they have chosen to keep it for the most serious crimes,” Hochman said.
“Until the law is changed, my office will continue to evaluate every death penalty-eligible case with the rigor, care and restraint these decisions demand.”
Other prosecutors argued the death penalty wastes state resources while failing to fight crime or make residents safer.
“By commuting death sentences, Governor Newsom will save California taxpayers hundreds of millions of dollars over the long term, and enable the state to continue its long-term investment into policies proven to improve public safety,” Contra Costa District Attorney Diana Becton said.
In recent years, governors in states like North Carolina, Oregon and Colorado have commuted death sentences for some or all inmates on death row. Most recently, Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey granted clemency in March to a man on death row for three decades.
Rev. Jeff Hood, a death row spiritual advisor, said he hopes more states will follow Newsom’s lead.
“The silence after the very breath of a human being is violently wrestled out of them during an execution is deafening. I’ve heard it fourteen times,” he told CNN. “Today, Governor Newsom has courageously chosen to break that silence.”

“I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values, undermines the foundations of our legal system, and diminishes each of us,” Newsom said in a public letter.
Newsom’s decision comes as he prepares to leave office after eight years and considers a run for president. The Democrat, who’s long been opposed to the death penalty, placed a moratorium on executions in California in 2019.
His latest move came after he realized “the limits of what government can justly accomplish,” he said.
Newsom moved to grant clemency to 548 people currently sentenced to death in California, of whom 529 are men and 19 are women, according to numbers provided by his office.
The state constitution requires the California Supreme Court’s approval to grant clemency to anyone convicted of a felony more than once, which means the court would have to approve 382 of those commutations, or roughly 70%, according to Newsom’s office.
According to the Death Penalty Information Center, Newsom’s action represents the largest mass clemency in American history. If they are all approved, it would reduce the U.S. death row population by nearly 30%, the center said.
California voters upheld the death penalty
Americans have long been divided over the death penalty. Nearly half of U.S. states have banned capital punishment outright, but executions are still carried out routinely around the country. On Thursday alone, Florida, Alabama and Indiana were scheduled to perform lethal injections.
Californians voted to uphold the death penalty in 2012 and 2016 ballot measures. No one has been executed in the state since 2006 and California has the largest death row in the Western Hemisphere.
Among the most notorious convicted killers on California’s death row are Richard Allen Davis, who kidnapped and murdered 12-year-old Polly Klaas in 1993, and Randy Kraft, the so-called “Scorecard Killer” who kept a list of his 16 victims in the 1970s and ’80s. Other prominent killers, including Scott Peterson and the Manson family members, received death sentences that were later commuted to life in prison.
Jess Nichol, Klaas’ sister, said she previously believed Davis deserved the death penalty, but her views evolved.
“The system tells survivors that execution matters to our healing,” Nichol said in a statement. “It doesn’t. It’s a distraction from what we actually need.”
Newsom said the decision was among the most difficult choices of his career because it will surface painful memories for crime victims’ families.
“As Governor, I alone bear responsibility for this decision and its impact, just as I alone would bear responsibility for each execution,” Newsom wrote.
The American Civil Liberties Union, which has said the implementation of the death penalty reflects racial bias, applauded the announcement.
“These commutations reflect what justice demands: an end to a racist, error-prone, and inhumane punishment that has burdened California for far too long,” Executive Director Anthony Romero said in a statement.
The ACLU is involved in an ongoing legal challenge to California’s death penalty statute, alleging it is racially discriminatory and unconstitutional.
Victims’ groups and prosecutors decry the decision
Patricia Wenskunas, founder of the California advocacy nonprofit Crime Survivors, which opposed the abolition of the death penalty, criticized Newsom’s decision.
“My heart hurts for every one of the victims and every one of their family members,” she said, calling the decision “offensive” and “outrageous.”
Steve Herr, whose son Sam Herr was murdered along with his friend Julie Kibuishi by Daniel Wozniak in 2010, said he was “absolutely disgusted” by the governor’s decision. He said the death of his son’s killer would have meant closure.
“When somebody commits such a heinous crime, they do not deserve to live,” Herr said. “To hear what Newsom just did … he’s just an outright coward.”
The California District Attorneys Association condemned the decision. Last month, the group sent a letter to Newsom expressing “grave concerns” about him considering the move and warning that such a sweeping action would inflict additional pain on victims’ relatives.
“With the stroke of a pen, Governor Newsom has disregarded the decisions of hundreds of jurors and judges, and the anguish of families who lost loved ones to the worst crimes imaginable,” CDAA President Jeannine M. Pacioni said in a statement. “The victims were never given a commutation. Their families were never given a choice. They deserve far better than this.”
San Luis Obispo County District Attorney Dan Dow called the move a “sickening abuse of power.”
Dow referenced Rachel Newhouse and Aundria Crawford, two women who were kidnapped, raped and murdered by Rex Allan Krebs in 1999, and Kesha Gurke, a 19-month-old girl tortured and murdered by Michael Whisenhunt in 1995.
“San Luis Obispo County juries sentenced both men to death. A unanimous California Supreme Court affirmed both judgments. Their families have waited decades for the State of California to keep its word. Today, the Governor broke it,” Dow said.
Orange County District Attorney Todd Spitzer also condemned the decision, calling it “mercy for the wolves and while inflicting the ultimate act of cruelty on the sheep.”
Other governors have taken similar actions
Newsom has said in the past that it is wrong for the government to kill its citizens and that capital punishment in practice has discriminated against mentally ill people and people of color.
Other governors have granted broad clemency to all death row prisoners in their states, including Gov. Kate Brown in Oregon in 2022 and Gov. Jared Polis in Colorado in 2020. Both are Democrats.
In 2024, President Joe Biden also granted clemency to 37 out of 40 federal prisoners sentenced to death.
Xavier Becerra, a Democrat who will take over from Newsom in January, has said he will extend the state’s moratorium on the death penalty.

California governor commutes sentences for state's 548 death row inmates
California Governor Gavin Newsom has commuted the death sentences of all 548 people on death row in the state, changing them instead to life in prison.
"We can now let these offenders die in obscurity while we forever remember and honour the victims," he said in a letter.
The decision to spare death row inmates is largely symbolic in a state that has not executed an inmate since 2006, though experts say it could save millions of dollars in court costs each year. Only 13 inmates have been executed since voters reinstated the death penalty in 1978.
The decision comes as Newsom, the Democratic leader of the most populous US state, has been discussed as a possible 2028 contender for president.
Newsom, who is term limited, is winding down his final months in office. Fellow Democrat Xavier Becerra is projected to take over after the midterm elections on Tuesday.
Newsom explained in his letter that he is exercising his constitutional clemency authority to commute the sentences to life without the possibility of parole.
"After nearly 30 years in public office, I have come to understand the limits of what government can justly accomplish," Newsom said. "I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California's values, undermines the foundations of our legal system and diminishes each of us".
California has historically had the largest population of death row inmates. Newsom had previously ordered a halt to the death penalty in the state in 2019.
Describing his decision as a difficult but "righteous action", Newsom said that although many Californians feel that those who commit brutal crimes deserve to die, he has concluded that "the state cannot morally kill them".
He said that by every measure, California's system for administering the death penalty "is a failure", and that it has not and cannot be fairly applied, resulting in the conviction of innocent people.
Life without the possibility of parole is the most severe punishment he can lawfully impose and that the state can ethically enforce, he said.
He acknowledged that his clemency action will anger and hurt some Californians and said that it will "always weigh heavily on me".
"As governor, I alone bear responsibility for this decision and its impact, just as I alone would bear responsibility for each execution," he wrote.
"For this reason, I am compelled to follow my conscience and, as authorised by our Constitution, take this action for the welfare of the State of California."
Because individual states have the power to prosecute crimes and order executions, much of the power lies with state governors.
Bernard E Harcourt, a law and civil liberties professor at Columbia University, told the BBC that it is not unprecedented for a potential presidential candidate to come out as an abolitionist in the run up to elections - despite the overall popularity of the death penalty in the US.
He noted that François Mitterrand did precisely that in his presidential campaign in France in 1981, taking "the higher ethical ground and was rewarded by the public for that".
"I detect a very similar ethical positioning in Governor Newsom's statements about the commutations. And here too, it may well be something that the voters respect," he said.
Newsom's decision comes after the high-profile botched execution of a woman in Tennessee in late September and while executions have been on the rise in the US. There are three executions scheduled for Thursday in Indiana, Florida and Alabama.
At least four of seven judges on the California Supreme Court will have to sign off on the commutations, CalMatters reported.
It is unclear how Newsom's decision will affect condemned inmates like Keith Doolin, 53, who was sentenced to death in 1996 for murdering two sex workers, Inez Espinoza and Peggy Tucker, and shooting four others. He maintains his innocence.
Doolin lived on death row at San Quentin for decades, until he was moved to another prison in 2025 when the governor announced the state would reform the prison for all but those on death row.
Doolin's mother, Donna Larsen, told the BBC that the news of Newsom's commutations - which includes Doolin - brought mixed emotions.
"At least the execution chamber will not be reconstructed, and no more killing by the people of the state of California," she said.
Anthony D Romero, the executive director of the American Civil Liberties Union, applauded Newsom's action.
"These commutations reflect what justice demands: an end to a racist, error-prone, and inhumane punishment that has burdened California for far too long," Romero said.
"By taking this step, Gov. Newsom has affirmed that the death penalty has no place in California and he showed real courage by confronting racialised injustice head-on."
Nathan Hochman, the top prosecutor in Los Angeles County, said that while Newsom has the power to commute sentences, only state legislature or voters can eliminate the death penalty.
"Californians have been asked on two separate ballot initiatives to abolish the death penalty and both times they have chosen to keep it for the most serious crimes," Hochman said in a statement.
On the federal level, President Donald Trump, a long-time supporter of the death penalty, has described capital punishment as "an essential tool for deterring and punishing those who would commit the most heinous crimes and acts of lethal violence against American citizens".
In 2020, during his first term, he ended a nearly two-decade moratorium on the federal death penalty, by ordering 13 executions over a six-month period.
While the moratorium returned under President Biden, on the first day of Trump's second term in 2025, he signed an executive order that re-instated the death penalty.
No federal executions have been carried out since he signed it, however. In the US, both the federal government and local states authorities can order executions.
The death penalty is legal in 27 states, but has been abolished in 23 states and Washington DC, according to the Death Penalty Information Center, a national non-profit.
California, which primarily uses lethal injection for executions, used to house male death row prisoners in San Quentin State Prison north of San Francisco, and female inmates in the Central California Women's Facility in the Central Valley.
But a 2016 ballot measure allowed for their transfer to other facilities that provide a necessary level of security, according to the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation.
