sources.news_title: ACLU Applauds Gov. Gavin Newsom’s Historic Commutation of All Death Sentences in California
sources.text:
SACRAMENTO – California Gov. Gavin Newsom announced today that he was moving to commute all death sentences in California, marking a historic step towards ending the death penalty in California and across the country.
The American Civil Liberties Union, ACLU of Southern California, ACLU of Northern California, ACLU of San Diego & Imperial Counties, and ACLU California Action joined the hundreds of organizations and individuals urging the Gov. Newsom to take this necessary step to address the persistent and systemic flaws with the death penalty in California.
Anthony D. Romero, executive director of the American Civil Liberties Union, issued the following statement:
“Today, Gov. Newsom made history by announcing his intention to commute every death sentence in California and clear the largest death row in the nation. In doing so, he honored his commitment to end a system that conflicts with human dignity, fairness, and the values enshrined in our Constitution.
“These commutations reflect what justice demands: an end to a racist, error-prone, and inhumane punishment that has burdened California for far too long. By taking this step, Gov. Newsom has affirmed that the death penalty has no place in California and he showed real courage by confronting racialized injustice head-on.
“The evidence against the death penalty has been overwhelming for decades. As the ACLU hand allies have documented in courts across the country, a person’s risk of execution is predictable, but for all the wrong reasons: race, geography, and politics. Such profound, systemic injustice demands a systemic response. Today, California comes closer to closing the chapter on a cruel and morally and legally corrupt practice and sets a powerful example for others to follow.”
Gov. Newsom’s announcement comes amid ongoing legal challenges to California’s death penalty system. In April 2024, the ACLU, alongside the NAACP Legal Defense Fund and the Office of the State Public Defender, brought a lawsuit challenging the state’s death penalty statute as racially discriminatory and unconstitutional under the Equal Protection guarantees of the California Constitution.
The evidence presented in that lawsuit revealed pervasive racial bias in California’s implementation of the death penalty. Black people are up to eight times more likely to be sentenced to death when compared to similarly situated non-Black defendants, while Latino people are at least six times more likely to be sentenced to death.
Under California law, the governor has the unilateral authority to commute death sentences in cases without additional felony convictions. For cases involving additional felony convictions, the governor’s commutation request now goes to the California Supreme Court for review and approval.
Additional statements below are from ACLU affiliates in California:
Abdi Soltani, executive director of the ACLU of Northern California:
“The death penalty has no place in California – or any society that values justice, fairness, and human rights. Our organization has fought for decades against this antiquated, inhumane system, and we applaud the governor for taking bold action to end it.”
Chandra Bhatnagar, executive director of the ACLU of Southern California:
“From its inception, California has imposed the death penalty in a racially discriminatory manner, creating a two-tiered system of justice. With this historic act of clemency, the state can turn the page — rejecting a broken, biased system and embracing a more just and equitable future for all.”
Norma Chávez-Peterson, executive director of the ACLU of San Diego & Imperial Counties:
“Systemic injustices call for systemic solutions. By granting universal clemency to all people with death sentences in California, Governor Newsom has joined a chorus of leaders nationwide who have rejected the death penalty and recognized it as a failed and unjust experiment. This isn’t about individual cases, it is about addressing a system that is racist, fundamentally flawed, ineffective, and unfixable.”

OUTGOING Governor Gavin Newsom said he will move to commute the sentence of over 500 inmates on death row to life in prison without the possibility of parole.
Newsom, who is scheduled to leave office in January 2027, said he made the decision because of his moral objection to the death penalty.
“This decision is among the most difficult of my career, not because I doubt its necessity for our state but because I know its announcement may surface excruciating memories for victims’ families,” Newsom wrote in a letter to Californians on Thursday.
“I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California‘s values, undermines the foundations of our legal system and remain true to our core values, first among them justice and human decency.”
There are 548 state prisoners on death row.
The mass pardon will apply to prisoners convicted of serious crimes.
The last time California conducted an execution was in 2006, when convicted murderer Clarence Ray Allen was put to death via lethal injection at the San Quentin State Prison.
The most recent historic commutations took place in 2024, when President Joe Biden commuted 37 federal death sentences before leaving office.
Biden also set a record on January 17, 2024 for the most commutations in a day as he reduced the sentences of nearly 2,500 people convicted of nonviolent drug offenses.
In 2003, Republican Illinois Governor George Ryan commuted 167 death sentences, just eight years before the death penalty was abolished in the state by Governor Pat Quinn.

Ryan told ABC affiliate WLS in 2023 that he had no regrets, saying, “I’m glad I did what I did. It cost me a few friends but that is the way it is.”
There were also four prisoners pardoned under Ryan. Newsom did not mention anything about pardoning death row inmates in his letter.
The largest non-death sentence pardon in the US was in 1977, when President Jimmy Carter pardoned around 200,000 Vietnam War draft evaders.
Newsom has the power to commute about 40% of the death sentences, but the remaining will require the state’s Supreme Court‘s stamp in order for it to be finalized.
The California constitution requires the state Supreme Court to approve clemency for anyone convicted of a felony more than once.
If the California Supreme Court allows Newsom to commute the prisoners, every condemned person will serve life without the possibility of parole, “the most severe punishment” the governor said he could lawfully impose.

The move comes just months before Newsom will leave office in California as he considers running for the White House in 2028.

“I do, however, pray that this action will finally separate the memories of the victims of these crimes from the fate of those who harmed them.”
Newsom said in his letter that he was following in the “moral leadership” of past presidents and governors across the country who have commuted death sentences.
Executive Director of the Death Penalty Information Center Robin Maher said Newsom’s announcement “marks a decisive moment in the history of the death penalty in the United States.”
“Though other governors have granted universal clemencies, none have been at this scale,” Maher said.
Newsom’s announcement also comes over a month after a botched execution took place in Tennessee with death row inmate Christa Pike.

Republican Governor-elect Marsha Blackburn told the Associated Press in October that Pike’s failed execution “should not be grounds to halt carrying out the death penalty.”

sources.news_title: Gavin Newsom to commute death sentence for 548 prisoners
Gavin Newsom spares every murderer on California's death row
Gavin Newsom seeks to clear death row, commutes sentences for hundreds of prisoners
sources.text:
In summary
Gov. Gavin Newsom commuted death sentences for 548 state prisoners, saying “state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values.” Victims rights advocates criticized his decision.
Gov. Gavin Newsom is commuting the death sentences of 548 people, clearing the California death row for the first time since the state conducted hangings in the late 19th century.
It is a monumental move in the history of capital punishment in America: The prisoners represent more than a quarter of the nation’s condemned inmates.
And it is a decision Newsom, a longtime opponent of the death penalty, has spoken about in starkly personal terms. In 2019, shortly after taking office, he issued a moratorium on executions and then dismantled the execution chamber in San Quentin State Prison. It was just three years after voters rejected a ballot measure to abolish the death penalty and instead approved one to speed them up. At the time, the governor said he couldn’t be responsible for killing another person.
“After nearly 30 years in office I have come to understand the limits of what government can justly accomplish,” Newsom wrote in a Thursday letter addressed “to all Californians.” “I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values, undermines the foundations of our legal system, and diminishes each of us.”
His anticipated decision garnered sharp condemnation in recent weeks from victims’ groups, who argued it flew in the face of juries and judges that had upheld the death sentences, and voters who have upheld the practice.
“I don’t think he or any person should undo the sentence rendered by a jury and signed off by a judge because of his personal beliefs or feelings,” said Topo Padilla, president of Crime Victims United, last week.
Since 2024, death row has been a metaphorical place. The male prisoners were cleared out of their individual cells in San Quentin and distributed among other 24 facilities. Twenty female prisoners condemned to death were moved to general population at the Central California Women’s Facility that year.
Even before Newsom’s 2019 moratorium, it had been more than a decade since the state performed an execution. His successor, Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra, has committed to extending the moratorium when he takes office. But a recent botched execution attempt in Tennessee and the Trump administration’s suggestion of televised executions has thrown the country into a renewed national debate over capital punishment.
It is not unusual for governors or presidents to commute sentences on their way out of office. Then-President Joe Biden commuted the sentences of 37 of the 40 federal death row prisoners in 2024. Newsom’s decision stands out as the largest act of mass clemency in U.S. history, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.
It comes as he decides whether to run for president after his term ends at the end of the year. Along with other signature Newsom moves like his early recognition of same-sex marriages as San Francisco mayor in 2004, it could boost his standing among Democrats as a bold actor pushing forward liberal causes, while inviting criticism from the center and right and from tougher-on-crime advocates.
Already, anti-death penalty groups have released an ad invoking Martin Luther King, Jr. that praises Newsom’s move as “rooted in justice, guided by conscience and made with courage.” Dan Newman, a Democratic strategist who works with those groups and also advises Newsom, said the governor made his decision without his political team and that Newsom did not know about the ad.
Most of the decisions Newsom made Thursday will need court approval. For those convicted of multiple felonies — nearly 400 prisoners — four of seven judges on the California Supreme Court will have to sign off on the commutations.
Anne Marie Schubert, chief executive of the Criminal Justice Legal Foundation and a former prosecutor, pledged that her group would challenge Newsom’s proposed commutations in the state Supreme Court. She said victims’ families were not notified of the proposed commutations.
“I find it atrocious and disrespectful and the most grotesque violation of victims’ rights I’ve ever seen,” Schubert said. “There’s 548 people on death row. That’s no less than 548 families that have been destroyed by what these people have done to their loved ones.”
Newsom said those with the commuted sentences will not be eligible for new Board of Parole Hearings commutation and resentencing regulations. That addresses some concerns prosecutors, victims’ groups and supporters of the death penalty had expressed as they anticipated Newsom’s decision: that those newly sentenced to life might get a chance later to be released.
“These offenders will die in prison but not by our hand,” Newsom wrote.
He said in his letter that the decision is among the most difficult of his career, “not because I doubt its necessity for our state but because I know its announcement may surface excruciating memories for victims’ families.” He said after meeting with them over the years, he considered commuting only some sentences but “that attempting to distinguish among crimes and offenders for clemency would inadvertently create two classes of murder victims — those whose perpetrators deserve the death penalty and then the rest.”
Last execution in 2006
California has not executed a prisoner since Arnold Schwarzenegger was governor. Tookie Williams in 2005 and Clarence Ray Allen in 2006 were the last to die by execution at San Quentin.
Newsom inherited a very different prison system than Schwarzenegger’s, marked by a rapidly decreasing incarcerated population. He moved to close five prisons so far, including a facility in Norco that was shut in October, and refashioned San Quentin as a hub for rehabilitation.
Natasha Minsker, former director of the American Civil Liberties Union of California’s Center for Advocacy and Policy, said the death penalty is now a forgotten part of California politics. “I’m shocked, when I talk to legislators and tell them to oppose it, they say we don’t have the death penalty in California,” she said.
Mary McComb, the former state public defender, said from her first case defending a man with intellectual disabilities who was charged with a capital offense, she has found a moral reason to oppose the death penalty.
“One can always hope, but without the commutations, it’s not always guaranteed that governors would continue to have the courage to (maintain a moratorium),” McComb said.
The most likely person to be sentenced to death is a Black or Latino person who kills a white person, according to a University of Miami study of California death sentences between 1987 and 2019. The study also found racial disparities were fairly consistent across California counties, though some counties’ juries were more likely than others to hand up a death sentence.
Riverside County hands down a disproportionate share of the state’s death sentences, according to the study.
“Even though the actual percentage differences outlined here are small given the rarity of death sentences, the magnitude of (geographic) disparities across counties is compelling and clearly points to several racialized death sentencing ‘hotspots,’ especially Riverside County,” wrote study author Nick Petersen.
That study and others that found racial disparities in death sentences were cited by the state public defender, which in 2024 filed a writ of mandate to Attorney General Rob Bonta, requesting that the state stop pursuing the death penalty in court or carry out executions.
One notable person filed a brief supporting that case: Gavin Newsom.
“California is not immune from the invidious influence of racial bias in its application of the death penalty,” Newsom wrote in the 2024 brief. “The nation’s capital punishment system is inextricably linked to the legacy of slavery and racial terror.”
Legacy of notorious killings
Newsom’s commutations will affect prisoners convicted in some of the state’s most notorious killings, including Richard Allen Davis, whose slaying of 12-year-old Polly Klaas shook the Bay Area in the 1990s; Charles Ng, who was convicted of killing 11 people in the Sierra Nevada foothills in the 1980s; and Scott Peterson; whose murder of his wife Laci Peterson in Modesto drove tabloid headlines.
In an interview before the decision was made, Polly Klaas’ father Marc Klaas said the prospect of the commutations “upsets me terribly.” In 1993 Davis kidnapped Polly as she was having a slumber party with friends in Petaluma and strangled her to death. He had prior convictions, and the case ushered in an era of tougher criminal sentencing and led politicians to push for the “Three Strikes” law.
After years of appeals, Klaas said he had already given up the expectation that Davis would be executed one day, at the time of Newsom’s moratorium.
“But I was still secure in my mind that he and the rest of them would be on death row for the rest of their lives,” he said. “It’s so discouraging. It makes me feel terrible and it regurgitates all my personal feelings.”
Davis’ case is among those that Newsom is submitting to the Supreme Court for approval.
Polly’s sister feels differently. She said in a statement Thursday that she used to think Davis deserved execution but came to realize that his killing won’t help her recovery or public safety.
“The system tells survivors that execution matters to our healing. It doesn’t. It’s a distraction from what we actually need,” said Jess Nichol.

Gov. Gavin Newsom told the California Supreme Court on Thursday that he will commute the death sentences of all 548 state prisoners awaiting execution, reducing their punishments to life in prison without parole.
Newsom can commute about 40% of the death sentences with the stroke of a pen, but the rest will require the high court’s approval in order to be finalized.
The mass commutation would apply to men and women convicted of some of the most heinous acts in the state’s history. Newsom and other opponents of capital punishment have long argued that the process is costly, cruel and discriminatory, with death sentences disproportionately handed down to defendants of color.
“I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values, undermines the foundation of our legal system, and diminishes each of us,” Newsom wrote in a letter to Californians explaining his decision. “I know we cannot execute people in our imperfect legal system and remain true to our core values, first among them justice and human decency.”
The move comes in Newsom’s final months as governor and as he considers a run for president. Reducing the death sentences could help him in a primary with a Democratic base of like-minded liberal voters, but potentially hurt him in a general election with a national electorate that supports capital punishment.
The decision to officially spare the condemned inmates is largely symbolic in a state that has not executed a prisoner since 2006, though experts say it could save millions of dollars in court costs every year. Only 13 inmates have been killed since voters reinstated the death penalty in 1978. The state’s electorate reaffirmed its support a decade ago, voting down a ballot initiative that would have abolished capital punishment. Polls show its popularity has waned in the years since.
Despite his outspoken opposition to state-sanctioned executions, the governor has declined to use his political influence with voters to pursue a ballot measure that would amend the state Constitution to align with his position and officially end the death penalty. Without changing state law, criminals can continue to be sentenced to death in California.
“California voters have voted to keep the death penalty on the books and I respect that,” Newsom wrote in the letter to Californians. “But the Constitution also gave every governor clemency authority, and that power exists for moments when law as applied cannot be squared with justice. For me, this is that moment.”
Newsom made national headlines two months after his inauguration in 2019 when he issued a temporary moratorium on executions and vowed to dismantle the death chamber at San Quentin State Prison, now called San Quentin Rehabilitation Center.
Calling the death penalty system a “failure,” Newsom said the punishment is also often reserved for poor people who cannot afford expensive legal representation, fails to deter crime and wastes taxpayer money.
Careful to avoid elevating a death penalty debate in the midterm elections, Newsom intentionally waited until after the general election on Tuesday to go a step further and launch the process of commuting all California death penalty sentences.
The decision is another bold signature Newsom move that sits well with his base of support in California and wealthy, white and college-educated national voters who would be crucial to his success in a Democratic presidential primary, said Mike Madrid, a Republican political consultant.
“Gavin’s exactly right with that base Democratic voter on that position,” Madrid said. “One hundred percent. It makes him a champion.”
However, his liberal stance on government executions could also create a vulnerability for him if he advances in the 2028 presidential election as the party’s nominee. More moderate blue-collar voters who helped the party flip Congress in the midterms, Madrid added, are “not in line with him on this.”
A poll conducted in August by the Pew Research Center found that about two-thirds of voters nationally favor the death penalty for people convicted of murder.
Those numbers could shift following the botched lethal injection of Christa Pike in Tennessee in September and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s now-scuttled plan to livestream the execution of Ft. Hood shooter Nidal Hasan by firing squad.
“Those events have really ripped the veneer off the death penalty in this country,” said attorney Natasha Minsker of the California Anti-Death Penalty Coalition. “The death penalty is an act of violence. It’s taking another life. I think that’s become clear to the entire country.”
The state spends more than $200 million a year to adjudicate automatic death penalty appeals and habeas corpus petitions for inmates who, in all likelihood, will never be executed, according to a 2025 report by the Habeas Corpus Resource Center.
The case of Clarence Ray Allen, the last inmate killed by lethal injection in California 20 years ago, is emblematic of how the law has failed, death penalty opponents say.
Allen was 76, making him the second-oldest person ever executed in the United States. He had been on death row for 23 years and his appeals cost the state more than $750,000. Many current condemned inmates are even older — some in their 80s and 90s — and their appeals even more drawn-out and expensive.
“It’s just a broken system,” said Michael Hersek, former executive director of Habeas Corpus Resource Center and an ex-state public defender.
Taxpayers foot the bill for both the defense and the prosecution in post-conviction capital cases, as well as the administrative judicial costs associated with years of complicated appeals in state and federal court.
The existing appeal requirements were instituted to counter long-standing racial bias in capital sentencing. Attempts to reform and expedite the appeals process over the years have further gummed up the system.
“There is no indication that the situation has improved, and ... [there are] data indicating that it has worsened,” Justice Leondra R. Kruger wrote for the California Supreme Court in 2024.
It’s estimated that death penalty appeals alone constitute about a quarter of the work of the California Supreme Court.
“It’s ludicrous, the amount of time, resources and energy put into these cases,” Hersek said.
Some victims’ families agree.
“The death penalty is this promise to people who are angry and broken that you’re somehow going to make them feel better by executing this person,” said Bethany Webb, whose sister Laura was among eight people killed in a mass shooting in Seal Beach in 2011.
Their mother was also badly injured in the attack.
“It is brutalizing to family members, the whole system,” Webb said.
More joined the chorus in the wake of the announcement.
“The system tells survivors that execution matters to our healing. It doesn’t. It’s a distraction from what we actually need,” said Jess Nichol, whose 12-year-old sister, Polly Klaas, was abducted from their Petaluma home and murdered in 1993, sparking a search that gripped the nation.
Others say Newsom’s latest move is a betrayal of the justice they were promised.
“It’s total disrespect for the victims. It’s a slap in the face,” said Sandy Friend, whose 8-year-old son, Michael Lyons, was abducted, raped and murdered in 1996.
She and other relatives stressed the unique brutality of many capital crimes, saying Newsom did not consider victims’ suffering when commuting their killers’ sentences.
“[Newsom] has a heart for criminals, I don’t think he has a heart for victims,” said Phyllis Loya, whose son, Larry Lasater, a police officer in Pittsburg, Calif., was killed in the line of duty by a man who was sentenced to death. “He doesn’t care about us.”
The commutations would go to inmates such as Charles Ng, who was convicted of killing six men, three women and two infant boys in Northern California in 1984 and 1985. Also in line to benefit is Klaas’ killer, Richard Allen Davis, who famously flipped cameras the bird after he was convicted. Another condemned inmate, Christopher Cheary, was convicted of murdering, raping and torturing his girlfriend’s 3-year-old daughter, Sophia Acosta, in Tulare County.
Former Sacramento County Dist. Atty. Anne Marie Schubert, the president and CEO of the Criminal Justice Legal Foundation and a death penalty supporter, said the families of murder victims had been “run over, torn up, and thrown in the garbage” by the commutations.
The governor decided that his personal opinion was more important than judges, juries and the will of the voters, she said, questioning why Newsom didn’t take action when he first took office instead of enacting a blanket reprieve on his way out as governor.
“It is perhaps the greatest travesty of justice I’ve ever witnessed,” Schubert said. “I think what’s particularly concerning is that the families of murdered children, killed police officers and [victims of] school shooters, mass shooters and baby killers — those families were not even given the decency of a phone call or a meeting or any kind of notice.”
Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra also opposes the death penalty. If state leaders wanted to resume executions, experts say it would take the better part of a decade and millions of dollars in new spending for the state to design and approve a workable protocol for lethal injections, rebuild a death chamber and secure the gray-market drugs necessary to perform executions.
Legal experts believe the end of the death penalty is likely inevitable in California, with or without Newsom’s involvement.
In 2024, the Office of the State Public Defender sued California Atty. Gen. Rob Bonta’s office, arguing “persistent and pervasive racial disparities infect California’s death penalty system.”
This spring, the California Supreme Court ordered Bonta’s California Department of Justice to show cause why it should not declare the death penalty unconstitutional — a move widely read as signaling the justices’ ultimate intent to end it.
“The statistical findings in the studies invoked by petitioners are extraordinarily disturbing,” Bonta wrote in his reply to the order in August. “Evidence of pervasive racial disparities in the administration of the death penalty could show that California’s capital punishment system gives rise to a constitutionally intolerable risk of arbitrariness.”
Among the 529 men and 19 women in line for commutations, around 60% would require review and approval by the California Supreme Court before Newsom’s term ends in January. Those cases involve prisoners who had a felony conviction on their record prior to receiving a death sentence, or racked up additional crimes while awaiting execution.
The high court previously rejected 10 clemency cases without much clarification when Gov. Jerry Brown submitted them in 2018 months before he left office.
If the mass commutation is approved by the California Supreme Court, the immediate effect could be relatively muted. The death chamber was taken down and all but a handful of the remaining condemned inmates were relocated from segregated housing in San Quentin to other facilities across the state after Newsom’s 2019 moratorium.
The decision to formally pause executions drew support from the late Pope Francis during Newsom’s 2024 trip to the Vatican, according to the governor’s retelling of a brief conversation between the two men.
In a subsequent interview, the governor said his Catholic background and the inequities in the criminal justice system influenced his refusal to sign off on executions. His father, the late William Newsom, also opposed the death penalty.
His father and grandfather were involved in the case of Pete Pianezzi, a friend who was wrongfully convicted of first-degree murder in the shooting and killing of a gambler and busboy in Los Angeles in 1937.
Pianezzi escaped the death penalty by a single vote and served 13 years in prison. He was later exonerated.
Even if it were possible to limit inequity and wrongful convictions in the criminal justice system, Newsom has said he would still be against the death penalty.
“The decision is among the most difficult in my career, not because I doubt its necessity for our state but because I know its announcement may surface excruciating memories for victims’ families,” Newsom wrote in the letter to Californians. “Today I am acting on my long and deeply held conviction that individually and collectively we are stronger as a society when we reject state-sanctioned killing.”
California politics editor Phil Willon contributed reporting.

SACRAMENTO, Calif. (AP) — California Gov. Gavin Newsom said Thursday that he’ll change more than 500 death sentences in the state to life in prison without the possibility of parole, though the state Supreme Court will have the final say in hundreds of those cases.
“I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values, undermines the foundations of our legal system, and diminishes each of us,” Newsom said in a public letter.
Newsom’s decision comes as he prepares to leave office after eight years and considers a run for president. The Democrat, who’s long been opposed to the death penalty, placed a moratorium on executions in California in 2019.
His latest move came after he realized “the limits of what government can justly accomplish,” he said.
Newsom moved to grant clemency to 548 people currently sentenced to death in California, of whom 529 are men and 19 are women, according to numbers provided by his office.
The state constitution requires the California Supreme Court’s approval to grant clemency to anyone convicted of a felony more than once, which means the court would have to approve 382 of those commutations, or roughly 70%, according to Newsom’s office.
California voters upheld the death penalty
Americans have long been divided over the death penalty. Nearly half of U.S. states have banned capital punishment outright, but executions are still carried out routinely around the country. On Thursday alone, Florida, Alabama and Indiana were scheduled to perform lethal injections.
Californians voted to uphold the death penalty in 2012 and 2016 ballot measures. No one has been executed in the state since 2006 and California has the largest death row in the Western Hemisphere.
Among the most notorious convicted killers on California’s death row are Richard Allen Davis, who kidnapped and murdered 12-year-old Polly Klaas in 1993, and Randy Kraft, the so-called “Scorecard Killer” who kept a list of his 16 victims in the 1970s and ’80s. Other prominent killers, including Scott Peterson and the Manson family members, received death sentences that were later commuted to life in prison.
Jess Nichol, Klaas’ sister, said she previously believed Davis deserved the death penalty, but her views evolved.
“The system tells survivors that execution matters to our healing,” Nichol said in a statement. “It doesn’t. It’s a distraction from what we actually need.”
Newsom said the decision was among the most difficult choices of his career because it will surface painful memories for crime victims’ families.
“As Governor, I alone bear responsibility for this decision and its impact, just as I alone would bear responsibility for each execution,” Newsom wrote.
Victims’ groups and prosecutors decry the decision
Patricia Wenskunas, founder of the California advocacy nonprofit Crime Survivors, which opposed the abolition of the death penalty, criticized Newsom’s decision.
“My heart hurts for every one of the victims and every one of their family members,” she said, calling the decision “offensive” and “outrageous.”
Steve Herr, whose son Sam Herr was murdered along with friend Julie Kibuishi by Daniel Wozniak in 2010, said he was “absolutely disgusted” by the governor’s decision. He said the death of his son’s killer would have meant closure.
“When somebody commits such a heinous crime, they do not deserve to live,” Herr said Thursday. “To hear what Newsom just did … he’s just an outright coward.”
The California District Attorneys Association didn’t immediately comment on the announcement. But last month the group sent a letter to Newsom expressing “grave concerns” about him considering the move and warning that such a sweeping action would inflict additional anguish on victims’ families.
“To simply erase all those judgments with the stroke of a pen, without considering the facts of each case or the families affected, would be a profound disservice to the administration of justice,” association President Jeannine M. Pacioni said.
San Luis Obispo County District Attorney Dan Dow called the move a “sickening abuse of power.”
Dow referenced Rachel Newhouse and Aundria Crawford, two women who were kidnapped, raped and murdered by Rex Allan Krebs in 1999, and Kesha Gurke, a 19-month-old girl tortured and murdered by Michael Whisenhunt in 1995.
“San Luis Obispo County juries sentenced both men to death. A unanimous California Supreme Court affirmed both judgments. Their families have waited decades for the State of California to keep its word. Today, the Governor broke it,” Dow said.
Orange County District Attorney Todd Spitzer also condemned the decision, calling it “mercy for the wolves and while inflicting the ultimate act of cruelty on the sheep.”
The ACLU applauds the move
The American Civil Liberties Union, which has said the implementation of the death penalty reflects racial bias, applauded the announcement.
“These commutations reflect what justice demands: an end to a racist, error-prone, and inhumane punishment that has burdened California for far too long,” Executive Director Anthony Romero said in a statement.
The ACLU is involved in an ongoing legal challenge to California’s death penalty statute, alleging it is racially discriminatory and unconstitutional.
Newsom has said in the past that it is wrong for the government to kill its citizens and that capital punishment in practice has discriminated against mentally ill people and people of color.
Other governors have granted broad clemency to all death row prisoners in their states, including Gov. Kate Brown in Oregon in 2022 and Gov. Jared Polis in Colorado in 2020.

Gov. Gavin Newsom moves to spare all 548 California death row prisoners
SACRAMENTO, Calif. — Gov. Gavin Newsom is preparing to spare the lives of the more than 550 people serving death sentences in California prisons, according to a letter obtained by The Sacramento Bee.
The New York Times reported last month that Newsom was considering the possibility of commuting the sentences of California’s 548 death row prisoners as one of his final acts as governor. Newsom is termed out of office in early January and is openly considering a run for president in 2028.
“After nearly 30 years in public office, I have come to understand the limits of what government can justly accomplish,” Newsom said in the letter. “I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values, undermines the foundations of our legal system, and diminishes each of us.”
Commuting a person on death row reverts their sentence to life without parole. As governor, Newsom can commute single-felony sentences, but must receive the California Supreme Court’s approval to commute sentences for people with multiple convictions.
Four of the seven justices must approve those requests, though there is no time limit for them to do so. If they do not approve before Newsom leaves office on Jan. 3, 2027, the requests lapse and do not roll over to the next governor, according to attorney Natasha Minsker, an anti-death penalty advocate.
“This would be the largest number of commutations in one go. California has one-quarter of all death sentences in the United States, the largest death row in the Western Hemisphere,” Minsker said. “So it would be by far the largest act of clemency, in a really historic move.”
In 2024, when former President Joe Biden commuted 37 prisoners facing the death penalty, advocates from the ACLU to Catholic bishops called upon Newsom to do the same.
Last week, the Rev. Dr. Jeff Hood, who advises men on death row, wrote to the governor to consider sparing death row inmates, calling it a “moral moment.”
“The silence after the very breath of a human is violently wrestled out of them is deafening,” Hood said in a statement Thursday. “I’ve heard it 14 times. Today, Governor Newsom has courageously chosen to break that silence. These commutations represent the height of moral leadership. Cruelty laid down. Now, I’m left with one prayer: God, don’t let any of the governors in the other executing states get any sleep until they find the ethical stamina to follow Newsom’s lead.”
California has not executed a prisoner in 20 years and the death penalty has been on hold since 2019, when Newsom issued a moratorium via executive order. At the time, he said the decision to pause executions was the result of a 40-year moral journey informed by his Irish Catholic faith. Newsom’s successor, governor-elect Xavier Becerra, said he would maintain the moratorium.
Newsom has opposed capital punishment since his days as San Francisco mayor, citing the death penalty’s burden on people of color and the possibility of executing innocent people. In 2008, he supported then-District Attorney Kamala Harris’ decision to pursue life without parole over the death penalty for Edwin Ramos, an undocumented gang member from El Salvador who shot and killed a father and his two sons in a case of mistaken identity.
As lieutenant governor, he supported two initiatives to repeal the death penalty. In 2020, he signed legislation that made it easier for prisoners to challenge their convictions over racial bias in their sentencings. In 2024, he discussed his death penalty opposition with Pope Francis I during a trip to the Vatican.
Black people make up almost a third of death row prisoners, despite comprising 5% of the state population. And additionally, the death penalty costs the state millions to implement, “causing a strain on our finances,” Minsker said. “That is money that’s not improving the lives of anyone in California. It’s certainly not making California a safer place, and that those are funds that should be redirected.”
While California voters have twice rejected repealing the death penalty, public support has waned nationwide in recent years. Tennessee recently paused the practice after prisoner Christa Pike, who was convicted of torturing and killing a classmate in 1995, survived two rounds of a botched lethal injection.
The California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation dismantled the death row chambers at San Quentin, the state prison that once held some of the U.S.’s most notorious prisoners, and renovated it into a rehabilitation center. The prisoners held there have been transferred to other state prisons.
Newsom’s blanket commutation request includes notorious prisoners like Charles Ng, Richard Allen Davis, and Cary Stayner. In July, the state Supreme Court upheld Stayner’s conviction and death sentence for killing four women in 1999 while working as a handyman in Yosemite.
Ng, along with his accomplice Leonard Lake, tortured and killed at least a dozen people at their Calaveras County cabin in the 1980s. Lake died by suicide after arrest and Ng fled to Canada. He was extradited in 1991 and sentenced to die in 1999.
Davis received the death penalty in 1996 for brutally kidnapping and killing 12-year-old Polly Klaas in 1993, after he had been released following convictions for other violent crimes. That helped bolster support for California’s three-strikes law, which voters approved in 1994.
Marc Klaas, Polly’s father, has since emerged as a Newsom critic, after the 2019 execution moratorium and more recently during the failed 2021 recall.
“Baby killers, cop killers, spree killers and serial killers have all found an ally in Gavin Newsom,” he told Fox News last month. “It’s unbelievable that he would side with the most heinous individuals in our society.”
The governor has crossed swords over public safety and criminal justice with members of his own party on a handful of occasions.
More recently, Newsom has resisted calls to fund Proposition 36, a ballot measure that levies harsher penalties for petty crime that voters overwhelmingly approved in 2024.
He opposed the measure at the time and behind the scenes his then-chief of staff, Dana Williamson, railed against a group of prosecutors led by former Ventura County District Attorney Greg Totten for not agreeing to delay the proposal to 2026, according to emails obtained by CBS Sacramento.
Williamson left Newsom’s office at the end of 2024 and pleaded guilty earlier this year to bank fraud, filing a false tax return and lying to the FBI for her role in a federal corruption scheme.
The coalition she sparred with, the California District Attorneys Association, came out against blanket commutation last month.

"This action will bring to a close these capital cases, some of which have been languishing in the courts for more than 40 years," Gov. Newsom said. "I acknowledge that this finality may bring comfort to some victims, but finality is not closure, something many victims have told me they never experience after a shattering crime."
The state constitution requires the California Supreme Court’s approval to grant clemency to anyone convicted of a felony more than once, which means the court would have to approve 382 of those commutations, or roughly 70%, according to Newsom’s office.
According to the Death Penalty Information Center, Newsom’s action represents the largest mass clemency in American history. If they are all approved, it would reduce the U.S. death row population by nearly 30%, the center said.
Other governors have granted broad clemency to all death row prisoners in their states, including Gov. Kate Brown in Oregon in 2022 and Gov. Jared Polis in Colorado in 2020. Both are Democrats.
Newsom shared on his podcast last month that he was considering commuting prisoners' death sentences before leaving office in January.
Newsom hinted at possible commutation in October
Dig deeper:
On the podcast, the governor mentioned the botched execution of Tennessee inmate Christa Pike, who received lethal injections twice – but lived.
"I have to prepare for my own consciousness test, my own rocking chair test," Newsom said in October. "Do I commute the largest death row in the western hemisphere?"
The prospect of a blanket commutation drew sharp pushback last month from death penalty advocates.
Reaction
What they're saying:
Representatives from Crime Victims United expressed outrage over the possibility of overturning outcomes reached through the judicial process.
"We are absolutely disgusted that this governor would be contemplating and most likely doing the commutation of people that are on death row when a judge and a jury have decided that that is the penalty," said Topo Padilla of Crime Victims United.
Padilla suggested Newsom's comments were driven by political ambition rather than legal or moral principles.
In an interview with KTVU, San Mateo County District Attorney Steve Wagstaffe also used the word "disgust."
"His focus is entirely 100% on the people who committed the crime," Wagstaffe said. "And he's not thinking of the victims' families. A total of 548 people, they're there because one or more victims existed in every case where somebody terminated a life. "
Specifically, Wagstaffe said that in 2016, California voters rejected a repeal on the death penalty. And so for Newsom to unilaterally make this decision, he said, is wrong.
"And what this does is that says, I'm throwing that aside because of my personal belief,'" Wagstaffe said. "I have trouble with that if we are truly a democracy. And I don't fault a governor if he has a case in mind. But to sweep with the broad brush that occurred here, that bothers me. I don't think that's democracy at work."
Meanwhile, the ACLU on Thursday praised the move, saying the commutations mark an end "to a system that conflicts with human dignity, fairness, and the values enshrined in our Constitution."
"These commutations reflect what justice demands: an end to a racist, error-prone, and inhumane punishment that has burdened California for far too long," said Anthony D. Romero, executive director of the ACLU. "By taking this step, Gov. Newsom has affirmed that the death penalty has no place in California and he showed real courage by confronting racialized injustice head-on."
Democratic strategist Dan Newman, who advises the governor, said Newsom has remained consistent through the years in his opposition to the death penalty.
"He listened to victims, studied what actually makes us safer, and did what he knew was right," Newman said.
He noted that eliminating the death sentence is not lenient by any means.
"Life without parole is hardly leniency. It means dying in prison, and in obscurity without the newsy spectacles of execution dates, candlelight vigils, and last meals," Newman said.
Last execution in California was in 2006
The backstory:
The last person to be executed in California was Clarence Ray Allen, an inmate at San Quentin State Prison who died by lethal injection on Jan. 17, 2006. He was convicted of three counts of first-degree murder with special circumstances in 1982.

SANTA ANA, Calif. – Orange County District Attorney Todd Spitzer on Thursday blasted Governor Gavin Newsom’s decision to commute the death sentences of all 548 inmates on California’s death row, calling the move a betrayal of crime victims and an affront to the juries that imposed those sentences.
In a statement released Thursday, Spitzer described the governor’s action as “mercy for the wolves” while inflicting “the ultimate act of cruelty on the sheep,” framing the debate as one between protecting offenders and delivering justice for victims and their families.
The commutation represents one of the most significant changes to California’s capital punishment system in decades. While California has largely suspended executions in practice for years, hundreds of inmates convicted of some of the state’s most notorious murders had remained under death sentences imposed by juries and upheld through extensive appeals.
Spitzer argued that the governor’s decision effectively nullifies verdicts reached by hundreds of juries throughout California.
“The decision to impose death is not one made by an elected District Attorney, an elected judge or an elected governor,” Spitzer said. “It is the only sentence that is handed down by a jury of 12 who have listened to all of the evidence and decided that imposition of death is what is just.”
The Orange County district attorney, whose office has historically been among the state’s most active users of the death penalty, vowed to continue seeking capital punishment in cases he believes warrant the ultimate sanction, despite Newsom’s opposition to executions.
Spitzer also tied the decision to broader criminal justice reforms enacted in California over the past several years. He contended that recent parole policy changes and efforts to reduce prison populations have weakened accountability for serious offenders and created uncertainty for victims’ families who believed offenders would spend the remainder of their lives behind bars.
Among the concerns cited by Spitzer:
- Victims’ families may feel that promises made during criminal prosecutions are being undone.
- Jury verdicts imposing death sentences have effectively been overridden by executive action.
- The governor’s action could become another step toward the eventual abolition of capital punishment in California.
- Families of homicide victims may now face renewed uncertainty regarding the future custody status of offenders.
Supporters of Newsom’s action, however, have long argued that California’s death penalty system has proven costly, inconsistent, and vulnerable to wrongful convictions. Death penalty opponents contend that life imprisonment without parole provides public safety while avoiding the risk of executing an innocent person.
The issue remains politically divisive in California. State voters have repeatedly rejected ballot measures that would have abolished the death penalty outright, while also approving measures intended to reform and speed up appeals in capital cases. At the same time, Newsom has consistently opposed capital punishment and previously imposed a moratorium on executions during his administration.
California’s death penalty debate stands in sharp contrast to several other Western states.
Among western states:
- Arizona continues to authorize and carry out executions, although the state has periodically paused executions amid legal and procedural reviews.
- Idaho retains the death penalty and has actively pursued executions of condemned inmates.
- Nevada maintains capital punishment under state law, though executions have become relatively rare.
- Utah not only retains the death penalty but also permits firing squads under certain circumstances if lethal injection drugs are unavailable.
- Texas, while not traditionally considered a Western state in the same regional grouping as California, remains the nation’s most active death penalty state and continues to carry out executions regularly.
- Oregon has largely halted executions and significantly reduced the use of capital punishment through executive actions and legislative reforms.
- Washington abolished its death penalty after the state supreme court found it was being applied in an arbitrary and racially disproportionate manner.
- Colorado repealed the death penalty in 2020 and commuted the sentences of the state’s remaining death row inmates.
For Orange County, the controversy is likely to reignite a long-running debate over public safety, victims’ rights, criminal punishment, and the role of executive power in California’s justice system.
What is certain is that Newsom’s action has drawn a fierce response from one of California’s most outspoken prosecutors. As the legal and political fallout unfolds, the divide between Sacramento’s criminal justice policies and many local law enforcement leaders appears as wide as ever.

By Sari Moon
California Gov. Gavin Newsom announced on November 5 that he will commute all 548 of the state’s death sentences to life without parole, calling state-sanctioned killing incompatible with California’s values. His office says the action covers 529 men and 19 women.
“We can now let these offenders die in obscurity while we forever remember and honor their victims,” he wrote in an open letter.

“I know we cannot execute people in our imperfect legal system and remain true to our core values, first among them justice and human decency,” he added.
The decision follows renewed national debate over the death penalty after the failed execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee. Pike survived after being administered two lethal doses of pentobarbital and was hospitalized in critical condition. The incident triggered international outrage and prompted renewed calls for a pause in executions across the country.

Men like Javier Righetti. He raped 15-year-old Alyssa Otremba, stabbed her more than 80 times, and set her body on fire near her home.

Here, a commutation needs a majority vote of the nine-member Pardons Board. That’s the governor, the attorney general, and the seven Supreme Court justices.
But don’t think nobody’s tried.
In December 2022, outgoing Democrat Gov. Steve Sisolak tried to commute all 57 of Nevada’s death sentences on his way out the door.
Sound familiar?
A Carson City judge stopped it. He ruled the board hadn’t given victims’ families the 15 days’ notice the law requires.
Sisolak ran out of clock. Ford won’t have that problem. He’ll have four years.
He’ll also have a fellow Democrat, Nicole Cannizzaro, sitting next to him on the Pardons Board as attorney general.
And he’s got another path: If the Legislature sends him a repeal bill, he’s already promised to sign it.
Gov. Lombardo vetoed a bill in 2025 that would’ve made executions harder. That veto pen leaves with Lombardo in January.
The Families Don’t Get a Vote
Here’s what gets lost in all the talk about “values.”
Families were promised justice. Juries delivered it. Then politicians decided they knew better.
Alyssa Otremba’s mother had to go to court in 2022 just to be heard. She shouldn’t have to do it again.
Newsom just showed us what a governor who opposes the death penalty does when he gets the chance.
Aaron Ford has told us he opposes it too.
Believe him.

sources.news_title: California Death Row: Newsom Moves to Commute 548 Sentences
sources.text:
California death row prisoners could soon have all 548 existing death sentences replaced with life in prison without the possibility of parole after Gov. Gavin Newsom announced a sweeping commutation effort on Thursday, November 5, 2026. The decision would represent the largest mass commutation of death sentences in modern American history, affecting 529 men and 19 women. However, hundreds of the sentence reductions still require approval from California’s highest court before becoming final.
Newsom announced the decision as he prepares to leave office in January 2027 after eight years as governor. His administration has already begun the process of replacing death sentences with life without parole, a punishment that would keep the affected prisoners incarcerated for the remainder of their lives.
The California death row announcement follows years of opposition to capital punishment from Newsom, who halted executions statewide in 2019. That temporary ban prevented the state from carrying out executions but did not eliminate existing death sentences. His latest action goes further by seeking to remove the possibility of execution for everyone currently sentenced to death in California.
Explaining his decision in a letter to Californians, Newsom argued that government executions conflict with the state’s values and undermine its justice system. He also acknowledged the pain the announcement could cause families who lost loved ones to violent crimes.
“As Governor, I alone bear responsibility for this decision and its impact, just as I alone would bear responsibility for each execution,” Newsom wrote.
Despite the sweeping announcement, the California death row commutations face a major legal requirement. Under the state constitution, a governor cannot grant clemency to someone convicted of a felony more than once without a recommendation from the California Supreme Court, supported by at least four justices.
Made to order and shipped to your door.
According to the Associated Press, 382 of the 548 cases require that additional approval. Newsom cannot finalize those commutations on his own, meaning the outcome will depend partly on the court’s decisions. Those who qualify for commutation without judicial approval face a different process.
If the entire effort succeeds, Newsom would surpass the previous modern record set in 2003, when Republican Illinois Gov. George Ryan commuted the death sentences of 167 prisoners shortly before leaving office. Ryan’s decision followed concerns about wrongful convictions and flaws in his state’s capital punishment system.
California death row has long been the largest in the United States. When Newsom announced his execution moratorium in March 2019, 737 prisoners were under death sentences. The state has not executed anyone since January 2006, when Clarence Ray Allen was put to death at San Quentin State Prison.
Only 13 prisoners have been executed in California since capital punishment was restored in the late 1970s, despite prosecutors securing hundreds of death sentences during that period. Years of legal challenges, mandatory appeals and disputes over execution procedures have contributed to the state’s lengthy death penalty process.
Newsom has repeatedly criticized both the fairness and expense of that system. When announcing the 2019 moratorium, he declared, “Our death penalty system has been, by all measures, a failure.”
Financial concerns also surround California death row. A 2025 report from the Habeas Corpus Resource Center estimated that the state spends more than $200 million annually handling capital appeals and related post-conviction proceedings. Those costs include legal representation, court proceedings, and reviews that can continue for decades.
Research by The Marshall Project and CalMatters has also identified racial disparities in California’s death sentencing practices. Their examination found that death sentences have been more common among Black and Hispanic defendants and that geography and prosecutorial decisions have influenced who receives capital punishment.
Those findings have helped fuel legal challenges questioning whether California’s death penalty system operates fairly. In 2024, the Office of the State Public Defender initiated litigation challenging racial disparities in capital punishment. The state’s highest court has since considered arguments over whether those disparities violate constitutional protections.
The prospect of commuting every California death row sentence has also drawn strong objections from some prosecutors and victims’ families.
San Luis Obispo County District Attorney Dan Dow publicly urged Newsom to reject blanket commutations in October, arguing that the state should consider each convicted person’s crimes and the impact on survivors individually.
“Justice is always individualized,” Dow said in his official statement.
Families have expressed different reactions. Sandy Friend, whose 8-year-old son Michael Lyons was murdered in 1996, criticized the move, telling the Los Angeles Times, “It’s total disrespect for the victims. It’s a slap in the face.”
Bethany Webb, whose sister Laura was killed in the 2011 Seal Beach mass shooting, offered a different perspective on years of capital litigation. Describing the death penalty process and its effect on survivors, she said, “It is brutalizing to family members, the whole system.”
The affected prisoners include people convicted in some of California’s most widely known murder cases, including Richard Allen Davis, who murdered 12-year-old Polly Klaas in 1993, and Charles Ng, who was convicted of multiple murders in Northern California during the 1980s. Any commutation would change their punishment, not overturn their convictions or make them eligible for parole.
California voters have also previously rejected efforts to eliminate capital punishment. Ballot measures seeking to repeal the death penalty failed in both 2012 and 2016. Newsom’s latest decision does not repeal the state’s death penalty law, which means prosecutors can still pursue capital sentences in future eligible cases.
The California death row decision arrives as Newsom’s political future draws national attention, including discussion of a possible 2028 presidential campaign. Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra has indicated he would continue the execution moratorium, but a moratorium alone would not provide the permanent sentence reductions Newsom is now pursuing.
For the 548 people covered by the announcement, the next major development will come through the clemency process and the California Supreme Court’s review of cases requiring approval. If every commutation is finalized, the state will have eliminated its existing death sentences while leaving capital punishment legally available for future cases.

Gavin Newsom, California’s governor, has commuted the death sentences of more than 500 people on the state’s death row on Thursday, a move that ensures they can never be executed under future administrations.
The Democrat’s mass commutation at the end of his term has converted all of the state’s death sentences to life without the possibility of parole, the largest clearing of any US death row in modern history.
The move comes after the failed execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee sparked global outrage and renewed calls for a nationwide pause on capital punishment.
His decision impacts 529 men and 19 women who were sentenced to death in the state, making up the largest death row in the western hemisphere, the governor said in a letter announcing his decision.
“I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values, undermines the foundations of our legal system, and diminishes each of us,” he wrote. “I know we cannot execute people in our imperfect legal system and remain true to our core values, first among them justice and human decency.”
Newsom, considered a probable candidate for president in 2028, has long opposed the death penalty and issued a moratorium on executions in 2019. He also dismantled the state’s physical death row chamber in the infamous San Quentin prison, transferring people with death sentences to other facilities where they had more freedom of movement and access to programs – for some, a dramatic change after decades isolated in solitary cells.
The last execution in California was in 2006, but hundreds of people incarcerated in the state’s prisons have continued to live under death sentences, making California home to the largest death row population in the nation.
Newsom’s office noted on Thursday that of the 548 people sentenced to death, 220 of them have waited 15 years or more to be appointed habeas counsel, the legal representation they are entitled to access to fight their cases. And 139 people have waited 20 years or more for representation. If there were no moratorium in place, there are 45 people in the state who are considered to have exhausted their appeals and would be immediately subject to execution.
“This decision is among the most difficult of my career, not because I doubt its necessity for our state but because I know its announcement may surface excruciating memories for victims’ families,” Newsom said. “I hold this painful truth along with the belief that this is a righteous action.”
Governors of both parties have taken bold measures to oppose capital punishment over the years, including an Illinois Republican who commuted all 167 death sentences in 2003 before leaving office. In 2024, North Carolina’s Democratic governor, Roy Cooper, commuted 15 death sentences in the state in his final day in office.
Support for the death penalty has been declining across the US, but Democrats at times have been reluctant to do mass commutations out of fear that Republicans will paint them as “soft on crime” politicians who sided with people convicted of brutal murders.
Newsom has supported criminal justice reform efforts, including changes to prioritize rehabilitative programs in prisons. But some advocates over the years have accused him of caving to political pressures on the issue, including when he has vetoed the release of high-profile prisoners even after they have been granted parole.
California is one of 27 states that still have the death penalty on the books.

sources.text:
(AP) — California Gov. Gavin Newsom said Thursday that he’ll change more than 500 death sentences in the state to life in prison without the possibility of parole, though the state Supreme Court will have the final say in hundreds of those cases.
“I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values, undermines the foundations of our legal system, and diminishes each of us,” Newsom said in a public letter.
Newsom’s decision comes as he prepares to leave office after eight years and considers a run for president. The Democrat, who’s long been opposed to the death penalty, placed a moratorium on executions in California in 2019.
His latest move came after he realized “the limits of what government can justly accomplish,” he said.
Newsom moved to grant clemency to 548 people currently sentenced to death in California, of whom 529 are men and 19 are women, according to numbers provided by his office.
The state constitution requires the California Supreme Court’s approval to grant clemency to anyone convicted of a felony more than once, which means the court would have to approve 382 of those commutations, or roughly 70%, according to Newsom’s office.
California voters upheld the death penalty
Americans have long been divided over the death penalty. Nearly half of U.S. states have banned capital punishment outright, but executions are still carried out routinely around the country. On Thursday alone, Florida, Alabama and Indiana had scheduled lethal injections.
Californians voted via ballot measures to uphold the death penalty in 2012 and 2016. No one has been executed in the state since 2006 and California has the largest death row in the Western Hemisphere.
Among the most notorious convicted killers on California’s death row are Richard Allen Davis, who kidnapped and murdered 12-year-old Polly Klaas in 1993, and Randy Kraft, the so-called “Scorecard Killer” who kept a list of his 16 victims in the 1970s and ’80s. Other prominent killers, including Scott Peterson and the Manson family members, received death sentences that were later commuted to life in prison.
Jess Nichol, Klaas’ sister, said she previously believed Davis deserved the death penalty, but her views evolved.
“The system tells survivors that execution matters to our healing,” Nichol said in a statement. “It doesn’t. It’s a distraction from what we actually need.”
Newsom said the decision was among the most difficult choices of his career because it will surface painful memories for crime victims’ families.
“As Governor, I alone bear responsibility for this decision and its impact, just as I alone would bear responsibility for each execution,” Newsom wrote.
Victims’ groups and prosecutors decry the decision
Patricia Wenskunas, founder of the California advocacy nonprofit Crime Survivors, which opposed the abolition of the death penalty, criticized Newsom’s decision.
“My heart hurts for every one of the victims and every one of their family members,” she said, calling the decision “offensive” and “outrageous.”
The California District Attorneys Association didn’t immediately comment on the announcement. But last month the group sent a letter to Newsom expressing “grave concerns” about him considering the move and warning that such a sweeping action would inflict additional anguish on victims’ families.
“To simply erase all those judgments with the stroke of a pen, without considering the facts of each case or the families affected, would be a profound disservice to the administration of justice,” association President Jeannine M. Pacioni said.
San Luis Obispo County District Attorney Dan Dow called the move a “sickening abuse of power.”
Dow referenced Rachel Newhouse and Aundria Crawford, two women who were kidnapped, raped and murdered by Rex Allan Krebs in 1999, and Kesha Gurke, a 19-month-old girl tortured and murdered by Michael Whisenhunt in 1995.
“San Luis Obispo County juries sentenced both men to death. A unanimous California Supreme Court affirmed both judgments. Their families have waited decades for the State of California to keep its word. Today, the Governor broke it,” Dow said.
Orange County District Attorney Todd Spitzer also condemned the decision, calling it “mercy for the wolves and while inflicting the ultimate act of cruelty on the sheep.”
The ACLU applauds the move
The American Civil Liberties Union, which has said the implementation of the death penalty reflects racial bias, applauded the announcement.
“These commutations reflect what justice demands: an end to a racist, error-prone, and inhumane punishment that has burdened California for far too long,” Executive Director Anthony Romero said in a statement.
The ACLU is involved in an ongoing legal challenge to California’s death penalty statute, alleging it is racially discriminatory and unconstitutional.
Newsom has said in the past that it is wrong for the government to kill its citizens and that capital punishment in practice has discriminated against mentally ill people and people of color.
Other governors have granted broad clemency to all death row prisoners in their states, including Gov. Kate Brown in Oregon in 2022 and Gov. Jared Polis in Colorado in 2020.
In 2024, President Joe Biden also granted clemency to 37 out of 40 federal prisoners sentenced to death.
Xavier Becerra, a Democrat who will take over from Newsom in January, has said he will extend the state’s moratorium on the death penalty.
